stem: A 34-year-old man comes to the clinic with deteriorating night vision. It is thought that he has an inherited defect in the retinal protein responsible for light perception in low-light conditions. Which of the following proteins is most likely defective?
explanation:
Rhodopsin
Rhodopsin is a cell membrane protein present in rod photoreceptors, and is responsible for initiating visual phototransduction, the conversion of light energy to an electrochemical response. Rhodopsin is responsible for enabling light in low-light conditions. Defects in rhodopsin are responsible for the condition retinitis pigmentosa manifesting as deteriorating night vision.

Cone opsin
Cone opsin is incorrect. Whilst rods are responsible for dark adaptation, cones are responsible for light adaptation. The photosensitive pigment in rods and cones is rhodopsin and opsin respectively. There are three types of cone opsin that respond differently to the same wavelength of light, with peak sensitivities to blue, red and green portions of the visible light spectrum. Defects lead to varying degrees of colour blindness.

Melanopsin
Melanopsin is incorrect. Melanopsin is a photopigment detected in retinal ganglion cells, of which there are five types with different functions, including regulation of circadian rhythms and pupillary responses.

Panopsin/Opsin-3
Panopsin or Opsin-3 is incorrect. This is a protein encoded by the Opsin-3 gene. This is largely expressed in tissues outside the eye, including the liver, testis, brain and pancreas.

Vertebrate-Ancient (VA) opsin
Vertebrate-Ancient (VA) opsin is incorrect. This is found in most vertebrate species, but not mammals. It is found in the inner retina, the pineal body and the habenular region of the brain.

stem: This could be due to which one of the following?
explanation:
A relapse of her lymphoma
Lymphomatous infiltration of the orbit is a rare but important differential when assessing orbital swelling. It will look like orbital cellulitis, but the patient will not be pyrexial or unwell. Swelling around the inferior rectus will cause reduced upgaze. Diagnosis is confirmed by biopsy of accessible tissues.

Conjunctivitis
Conjunctivitis is incorrect. This does not restrict eye movement, and is associated with diffuse redness of the affected eye and discharge.

Orbital cellulitis
Orbital cellulitis is incorrect. The patient is off chemotherapy, is apyrexial and is not unwell.

Scleritis
Scleritis is incorrect. This would cause only minimal lid oedema and is typically painful, associated often with reduced visual acuity.

Uveitis
Uveitis is incorrect. This is associated with inflammation of the iris, blurry vision and is a common feature in systemic disease. Non-Hodgkin’s.

stem: A 26-year-old man with aortic regurgitation is referred from the Cardiology Department to the Eye Clinic to look for features of Marfan syndrome. Which one of the following ocular features suggests the diagnosis?
explanation:
Dislocated lenses
Ocular features suggesting a diagnosis of Marfan syndrome include: Lens dislocation (classically upwards) High myopia Peripheral retinal degeneration, with a risk of retinal detachment.

High hyperopia
High hyperopia is incorrect. Hyperopia refers to being long sighted, and is not associated with Marfan syndrome.

Band keratopathy
Band keratopathy is incorrect. Band keratopathy is an abnormal accumulation of calcium deposits on the cornea, usually from recurrent corneal disease, but can also be related to hypercalcaemia.

Raised intraocular pressure
Raised intraocular pressure is incorrect. Raised ocular pressure is not associated with Marfan syndrome.

Retinitis pigmentosa
Retinitis pigmentosa is incorrect. stem: A 71-year-old man presents with deteriorating vision. He complains of blurred central vision when looking through both eyes, although the left eye is slightly worse than the right. Fluorescein angiography shows choroidal neovascularisation with leakage at the macula in both eyes. When assessing possible risk factors for his condition, which one of the following is the most important?
explanation:
Smoking
Smoking, hypertension and previous cataract surgery have all been implicated in the pathogenesis of agerelated macular degeneration (ARMD), but smoking is regarded as the most important modifiable risk factor. Important non-modifiable risk factors include white European ethnicity and a positive family history. Recent studies have pointed to genetic differences in the complement pathway having an important role to play in the pathogenesis of the condition. Anti-vascular endothelial growth factor (anti-VEGF) therapies have recently been introduced for the treatment of exudative (wet) ARMD. There remains no effective treatment for non-exudative (dry) ARMD.

Alcohol
Alcohol is incorrect. It is not a risk factor.

Cataract surgery
Cataract surgery is incorrect. This increases the risk of ARMD, but is not as significant as smoking.

Diabetes
Diabetes is incorrect. Diabetic retinopathy can present a similar appearance on ophthalmoscopy, with neovascularisation, especially at the macule, having significant impact on sight. However, this is an advanced presentation of diabetic retinopathy and with no other features of diabetic involvement of the eye, the most likely diagnosis is wet ARMD.

Hypertension
Hypertension is incorrect. This also increases the risk of ARMD, but not as significantly as smoking. He is a contact lens wearer and he has pain, photophobia and decreased vision in his left eye after accidentally leaving his contact lens in situ overnight. He wears monthly soft lenses and admits he does not clean them each time before and after use. On examination he has reduced visual acuity in the left eye to 6/24, with diffuse conjunctival injection and corneal haze. stem: A 22-year-old man with ulcerative colitis and chronic lower back pain complains of a red and painful eye. Which one of the following is likely to be present on examination of his eyes?
explanation:
Cells in the anterior chamber
Patients with ulcerative colitis and possibly ankylosing spondylitis have a higher risk of anterior uveitis, due to the HLA-B27 association. Anterior uveitis on examination manifests as conjunctival injection, cells and flare in the anterior chamber and photophobia. There may or may not be keratic precipitates, fibrin, synechiae and a hypopyon.

Purulent discharge
Purulent discharge is incorrect. Purulent discharge is a feature of conjunctivitis, usually bacterial. The eye may be uncomfortable but is not usually painful.

A dilated pupil
A dilated pupil is incorrect. The patient may be treated with mydriatrics in anterior uveitis, but in the first presentation the pupil would not be dilated.

Profound visual loss
Profound visual loss is incorrect. Acute anterior uveitis does not usually manifest as profound visual loss. Visual acuity is usually preserved or slightly reduced. Uveitis A patient presents with a first episode of a painful reduction in visual acuity in one eye. The acuity is 6/60, ocular movements produce pain and the optic disc is normal. Which one of the following investigations supports the diagnosis of optic neuritis?

Retinal haemorrhages
Retinal haemorrhages is incorrect. Retinal haemorrhages are not a feature of acute anterior uveitis, although they may occur in posterior uveitis associated with conditions such as sarcoidosis.

stem: A 40-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis takes oral steroids. She presents with watering of both eyes associated with intermittent blurred vision when using a computer. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Dry eyes
Rheumatoid arthritis is associated with dry eyes. Tear-film integrity on the corneal surface is required both for comfort and to provide an optically smooth surface for refraction. Therefore, in dry eye, when the tear film cannot provide adequate wetting of the corneal surface between blinks, grittiness and intermittent blur occurs. A reflex response to irritation of the corneal surface is epiphora, or watering. Symptoms will be worse when tear-film evaporation is greater, for example in windy or in warm, dry (air-conditioned air) environments, or when the blink rate declines (as is likely when concentrating on computer work). The setting and recurrent nature of the intermittent blurring points towards ocular surface dryness as opposed to other forms of transient visual loss, such as transient ischaemic attacks (TIAs).

Cataract
Cataract is incorrect. Systemic or topical steroid treatment can cause ocular side-effects. Steroid use is a cause of cataract in young or middle-aged patients. A ‘steroid cataract’ is typically posterior subcapsular, and causes constant and gradually progressive blur. Cataract does not cause watery eyes, and while visual symptoms can vary, visual impairment is usually constant.

Diabetic retinopathy
Diabetic retinopathy is incorrect. Steroids can cause raised blood glucose levels. Fluctuating blood sugar levels can cause osmotic swelling of the lens in the eye, resulting in fluctuations in vision. However, diabetic retinopathy will not affect vision unless maculopathy occurs (oedematous, exudative, ischaemic or mixed) or vitreous haemorrhage occurs. Furthermore, the visual symptoms with diabetic retinopathy are not usually intermittent.

Glaucoma
Glaucoma is incorrect. Occasionally, topical or systemic steroid use results in raised intraocular pressure, with subsequent progressive damage to the optic nerve and peripheral vision (secondary open-angle glaucoma). However, any visual symptoms due to peripheral visual field loss would not be intermittent. (The rise in intraocular pressure usually reverses when steroid treatment is stopped. Any damage to the optic nerve and visual field, however, would not be reversible).

Transient ischaemic attack.

stem: A patient is seen with features of proliferative retinopathy in one eye and background diabetic retinopathy in the other. Which one of the following tests is most likely to provide an explanation?
explanation:
Carotid Doppler ultrasound
Asymmetric diabetic retinopathy should raise a suspicion of ocular ischemic syndrome (OIS) on the side affected worse. OIS is usually due to atherosclerosis, in those aged 50 or over. It is frequently under-diagnosed as it has non-specific signs involving the anterior and posterior segment. It manifests as visual loss with or without pain, with signs including raised intraocular pressure, rubeosis iridis, anterior chamber cells, cataract, retinal haemorrhages, neovascularisation of the disc and retina, cotton-wool spots and micro-aneurysms. Typically, veins are dilated but non-tortuous, unlike in central retinal vein occlusion. Fluorescein angiography and carotid Doppler ultrasound are the investigations of choice, the latter typically showing >90% obstruction of the carotid artery. Cardiovascular risk factors should be identified and optimised.

Chest X-ray
Chest X-ray is incorrect. Ocular ischaemic syndrome does not have respiratory manifestations, and a chest X-ray would not provide relevant diagnostic information.

Electrocardiography
Electrocardiography is incorrect. An ECG (electrocardiogram) may show atrial fibrillation, or other arrhythmias which need to be identified and treated, but this is not diagnostic of ocular ischaemic syndrome.

Coagulation screen
Coagulation screen is incorrect. This should form part of the cardiovascular work-up in someone identified as having OIS, but again is not diagnostic.

24-hour urinary protein
24-hour urinary protein 24 h urinary protein is incorrect.

stem: A diabetic patient with diplopia is found to have a IIIrd nerve palsy. Which one of the following clinical features suggests that urgent neuroimaging should be carried out?
explanation:
Pupil involvement
The third cranial nerve has motor fibres to the levator palpabrae superioris, superior, medial and inferior recti, inferior obliques as well as pupillomotor fibres to the iris sphincter. Depending on the cause of IIIrd cranial nerve palsy, the function of the iris sphincter can either be spared or affected. If the pupil is spared, an ischaemic cause is more likely (check the individual’s likely cardiovascular profile, in this case diabetes makes this more likely). If the pupil is involved, a compressive lesion must be suspected, particularly if there is associated pain. This warrants urgent intracranial scan and, if appropriate, onward referral to neurosurgery.

Impaired adduction
Impaired adduction is incorrect. Impaired adduction is a manifestation of a IIIrd cranial nerve palsy but does not necessarily warrant urgent investigation (unlike pupil involvement).

Impaired elevation
Impaired elevation is incorrect. Impaired elevation is a manifestation of a IIIrd cranial nerve palsy but does not necessarily warrant urgent investigation (unlike pupil involvement).

Nystagmoid jerks
Nystagmoid jerks is incorrect. Jerk nystagmus is not a feature of IIIrd cranial nerve palsy and can be seen under physiological conditions or in infantile nystagmus.

stem: A 30-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department with a fourth episode of painful reduction in visual acuity in one eye. Her acuity is 6/60, ocular movements produce pain and the optic disc is hyperaemic. Which investigation is most likely to suggest that her optic neuritis is due to multiple sclerosis (MS)?
options: Abnormal visual evoked potentials (VEP) in the contralateral eye
Bilateral spike and wave activity on the electroencephalogram (EEG)
explanation:
Abnormal visual evoked potentials (VEP) in the contralateral eye
Abnormal visual evoked potentials (VEP) in the contralateral eye are correct. MS is characterised by lesions that are disseminated in both space and time. VEPs measure the electrical activity in the brain in response to visual stimuli and can detect subclinical lesions along the visual pathways. The presence of an abnormal VEP in the contralateral eye suggests the presence of additional CNS lesions, making the diagnosis of MS more likely.

Abnormal nerve conduction studies
Abnormal nerve conduction studies are incorrect as MS primarily affects the central nervous system (CNS) rather than the peripheral nervous system. Nerve conduction studies evaluate the function of peripheral nerves and would not typically show abnormalities in patients with MS. Therefore, this investigation would not provide useful information for diagnosing MS. In MS, the pathology involves demyelination within the CNS, which nerve conduction studies cannot detect.

Xanthochromia in the CSF
Xanthochromia in the CSF is incorrect because it is typically associated with subarachnoid haemorrhage, not MS. In MS, cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis might show oligoclonal bands and mild lymphocytosis, but not xanthochromia. Xanthochromia indicates the presence of blood breakdown products in the CSF, which is not a feature of MS. Therefore, this finding would not support the diagnosis of MS.

Normal MRI brain scan
An MRI scan is one of the most important diagnostic tools for MS, as it can reveal characteristic plaques or lesions in the brain and spinal cord. A normal MRI would not support the diagnosis of MS, as it would lack the evidence of demyelinating lesions typically seen in this disease. Therefore, a normal MRI would make MS less likely rather than more likely. Optic Neuritis A 32-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis presents to the Rheumatology Clinic with a complaint of severe pain and reduced vision in one of her eyes. The medical specialist trainee notes that one eye is dusky red in colour and that the vision in this eye is reduced to 6/36. What is the appropriate management?

Bilateral spike and wave activity on the electroencephalogram (EEG)
Bilateral spike and wave activity on the EEG is incorrect. EEG findings are of limited value in diagnosing MS, as they are more commonly associated with epilepsy and other seizure disorders. MS does not typically cause the specific EEG patterns seen in seizure activity. Therefore, EEG is not a useful investigation for diagnosing MS in this context.

stem: A 20-year-old woman presents with gradually reducing vision in her left eye of two weeks' duration. She has some discomfort moving her eye from one side to another. Visual acuity is 6/4 (right eye) and 6/36 (left eye). The left pupil reacts sluggishly to light and the consensual pupillary reaction in the right eye is also sluggish. Optic discs are normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Retrobulbar neuritis
As the optic discs appear normal, it might be tempting to pass off the blurring as factitious. However, in retrobulbar neuritis it is said that ‘the patient sees nothing and the doctor sees nothing’. As the inflammation is behind the optic nerve head (ie retrobulbar), as opposed to optic neuritis, the optic nerve head or optic disc appears normal. Symptoms and signs of retrobulbar neuritis: Optic nerve function is affected in the same way in patients with optic neuritis and retrobulbar neuritis. The visual acuity will be reduced to a very variable degree, and a relative afferent pupillary defect will be apparent during the ‘swinging flashlight test’. Colour vision will be reduced to a greater extent than might be predicted from visual acuity. Red desaturation – ie when red looks more washed out to one eye than the other – is a sensitive sign of optic nerve dysfunction. Visual field defects will occur, typically a central scotoma, but the type of defect varies. An episode of optic or retrobulbar neuritis can contribute to a diagnosis of multiple sclerosis, if other neurological episodes separated in time and site occur.

Cerebral tumour
Cerebral tumour is incorrect. A compressive optic neuropathy, such as from a cerebral tumour, is an important differential of a unilateral optic neuropathy.

Holmes–Adie pupil
Holmes-Adie pupil is incorrect. Holmes–Adie pupil is an idiopathic condition, typically affecting young women, presenting with an enlarged pupil that is poorly reactive to light and only sluggishly accommodates. Absent ankle jerks are a frequent association. The consensual pupil reflex is typically unaffected.

Factitious visual loss
Factitious visual loss is incorrect. While a demyelinating optic neuritis would be by far the commonest cause of vision loss in this case (a young female), if the vision did not make a recovery as typically occurs in optic neuritis, further investigation to rule out other causes such as compression would be warranted.

Parinaud syndrome
Parinaud syndrome is incorrect. Parinaud syndrome is caused by a lesion in the dorsal midbrain, and causes a variety of signs, including mid-dilated pupils, upper lid retraction and paralysis of upward gaze. It does not typically cause an afferent pupillary defect or unilateral reduction in visual acuity.

stem: A 65-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with sudden onset of vision loss in his right eye. On examination, he has a relative afferent pupillary defect and a cherry-red spot on fundus examination. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Central retinal artery occlusion
Central retinal artery occlusion (CRAO) presents as sudden painless monocular vision loss accompanied by a relative afferent pupillary defect due to ischemia of the retina's inner layers supplied by the central retinal artery. A cherry-red spot at the macula is observed because of underlying normal choroidal circulation, and it stands out against the pale retina caused by ischemia. This condition requires urgent attention as it indicates mostly an embolic or thrombotic event affecting ocular perfusion.

Acute angle-closure glaucoma
Acute angle-closure glaucoma typically presents with severe ocular pain, headache, nausea and vomiting, along with a red eye and cloudy cornea on slit-lamp examination. Intraocular pressure is markedly elevated in acute angle-closure glaucoma, which can lead to rapid vision loss if not treated promptly. The presence of a relative afferent pupillary defect and cherry-red spot on fundus exam are not characteristic findings of acute angle-closure glaucoma.

Optic neuritis
Optic neuritis often causes painful vision loss associated with ocular movements and may be accompanied by other neurological symptoms suggestive of multiple sclerosis or other demyelinating diseases rather than the painless visual loss with abrupt onset presented here.

Ocular ischaemic syndrome
Chronic vascular insufficiency that might affect both anterior segments (eg rubeosis iridis leading to neovascularisation of the iris) and posterior segment changes, including mid-peripheral haemorrhages, but typically does not exhibit sudden onset painless visual loss seen in CRAO cases.

Retinal detachment
Retinal detachment commonly presents with photopsias (flashes of light) and floaters followed by peripheral field defects progressing towards central visual impairment if the macula becomes detached. However, it lacks clinical signs such as relative afferent pupillary defect or characteristic fundoscopic appearance like cherry-red spot indicative more towards arterial occlusive processes rather than mechanical separation of neurosensory retina from the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) layer. Retinal Artery OcclusionA 19-year-old man with Ehlers-Danlos Type IV comes to the Emergency Department because of acute painless loss of vision in his right eye. He had normal vision (6/6) in both eyes until he awoke on the morning of presentation, where his vision had deteriorated to count fingers. Examination of the left eye is normal. Anterior segment examination of the right eye was normal.

stem: A teenager is referred by his optometrist with a diagnosis of Lisch nodules of the iris. What is the most likely sign you might observe on examination?
options: Haemorrhagic telangiectasia of the skin and buccal mucosa
explanation:
Axillary freckles
The phakomatoses are congenital ectodermal dysplasias, in which benign tissue overgrowth occurs. Neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF-1) is inherited in an autosomal dominant fashion, but has variable expressivity and irregular penetrance. Lisch nodules are golden nodules on the iris occurring bilaterally in the teenage years onwards in NF-1; they are a specific sign, and referral to an ophthalmologist to look for them using a slit lamp can help in diagnostically uncertain cases. Also in NF-1, axillary freckles appear at 10 years of age, while café au lait spots increase in size and number throughout childhood.

Ash-leaf spots on the trunk
Ash-leaf spots on the trunk is incorrect. Ash-leaf spots occur in tuberous sclerosis.

Ectopia lentis
Ectopia lentis is incorrect. While ectopia lentis (subluxation or dislocation of the lens from its usual position in the eye) has congenital causes (such as Marfan syndrome) and acquired causes (such as ocular trauma), it is not a typical feature of neurofibromatosis.

Haemangioblastoma of the spinal cord
Haemangioblastoma of the spinal cord is incorrect. Haemangioblastomata of the spinal cord and cerebellum, pons and medulla can occur in von Hippel–Lindau disease. NeurofibromatosisHaemorrhagic telangiectasia of the skin and buccal mucosa
Haemorrhagic telangiectasia of the skin and buccal mucosa is incorrect. Osler–Weber–Rendu syndrome is characterised by haemorrhagic telangiectasia in the skin, mucous membranes and viscera.

stem: A 34-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department with redness and mild discomfort in her right eye that has been present for two days. She reports no vision changes, discharge or trauma. On examination, there is sectoral redness of the conjunctiva with a mild tenderness on palpation, but her visual acuity is normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Episcleritis
Episcleritis is characterised by the acute onset of unilateral or bilateral red eye associated with mild discomfort but without significant pain or vision loss, matching this patient's presentation. Sectoral redness of the conjunctiva and mild tenderness are typical findings in episcleritis due to inflammation confined to episcleral tissue without deeper scleral involvement.

Anterior uveitis
This condition typically presents with more significant symptoms such as photophobia, pain and sometimes decreased visual acuity. Additionally, anterior uveitis often shows circumcorneal (ciliary) injection rather than sectoral redness observed in this patient. The presence of cells in the anterior chamber is the hallmark of anterior uveitis and can also be seen on slit-lamp examination, which was not mentioned here.

Bacterial conjunctivitis
Bacterial conjunctivitis usually presents with a purulent discharge rather than the watery discharge of viral or allergic conjunctivitis and matting of the eyelids upon waking up, which was not reported by this patient. Eyelid oedema is often present. Moreover, bacterial conjunctivitis typically does not cause tenderness on palpation.

Keratitis
Keratitis generally causes severe pain along with photophobia and decreased vision, which were absent in this case history. Furthermore, keratitis often involves corneal involvement that may be detected as corneal infiltrates or ulceration upon slit-lamp examination, which was not noted here. EpiscleritisScleritis
Scleritis usually presents with severe ocular pain that can radiate to surrounding facial structures and is often associated with a deep violaceous hue due to scleral vessel congestion – features missing from this patient. It also typically affects vision more significantly than described here since it involves deeper ocular tissues compared to episcleral inflammation seen in episcleritis.

stem: A 70-year-old woman presents with sudden loss of vision in one eye. Which of the following clinical findings most commonly suggests a diagnosis of giant-cell arteritis (GCA)?
explanation:
Optic disc swelling
Giant cell arteritis (GCA) affects the large and medium-sized arteries. Occlusive vasculitis causes optic nerve ischaemia, manifesting as optic disc swelling and leading to sudden, unilateral visual loss. This condition is known as ‘arteritic anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy’ (AION). ESR is typically raised, with new-onset headache and temporal artery tenderness. Other symptoms of GCA include jaw claudication, scalp tenderness, weight loss, loss of appetite and polymyalgia rheumatica. It is an ophthalmic emergency and steroids must be initiated immediately to help prevent visual loss in the contralateral eye. A temporal artery biopsy may be performed to confirm the diagnosis.

Central retinal artery occlusion (CRAO)
Central retinal artery occlusion (CRAO) is incorrect. This may be a manifestation of GCA, with occlusive vasculitis of the central retinal artery, and should always be considered in patients over the age of 50 in particular presenting with sudden visual loss. This is not as common as optic disc swelling, which would strongly raise suspicion of GCA in an elderly patient with symptoms and signs as mentioned.

Isolated central scotoma
Isolated central scotoma is incorrect. GCA normally causes total, sudden visual loss. A central scotoma would be consistent with macular disease.

Uveitis
Uveitis is incorrect. Uveitis usually manifests as a red eye, with cells in the anterior chamber plus or minus a hypopyon, vitritis and retinitis, none of which are present in GCA. Patients may complain of eye pain on the affected side in GCA, and so a slit-lamp examination of the anterior and posterior segments is required to narrow the differential diagnosis. 812 Giant Cell Arteritis A 30-year-old man, under investigation for abdominal cramps and passing blood rectally, presents with an acutely painful, red and photophobic eye.

Raised intraocular pressure (IOP)
Raised intraocular pressure is incorrect. GCA does not typically cause raised intraocular pressure, which is usually related to glaucoma or neovascularisation.

stem: A 48-year-old Chinese man presents urgently to you via his GP. He tells you that he was due to see you in the clinic the next week because six weeks ago he experienced painless loss of vision in his right eye, which progressed over a two-week period such that now he is only able to see shadows out of that eye. Over the last two days, the vision has deteriorated in his left eye and this has prompted his urgent referral. His past medical history is that he is hypertensive and had a nasal sinus carcinoma treated with radiotherapy two years ago. On examination his visual acuities are hand movements right, 6/12 left. He has a right relative afferent pupillary defect and his right optic nerve is pale. There are no other physical signs. An urgent computed tomography (CT) scan is performed, which shows no abnormality of the anterior visual pathway. What is the likely diagnosis?
options: Tumour recurrence too small to be resolved by CT
explanation:
Radiation optic neuropathy
The examination findings point to an abnormality of the anterior visual pathway. Radiation optic neuropathy is an ischaemic disorder of the optic nerve that classically occurs months to years after radiation to the brain, orbits or paranasal sinuses. This results in progressive and profound irreversible visual loss that is often sequential. The onset can be within a few months of the radiation, with a peak at 1.5 years.

Demyelinative optic neuropathy
Demyelinative optic neuropathy is incorrect. This typically occurs as a presenting symptom of multiple sclerosis and is associated with decreased visual acuity, specifically colour loss, and pain on eye movements. It would be unusual to have such profound visual loss, and some recovery usually occurs.

Metastases in the occipital cortices
Metastases in the occipital cortex is incorrect. These would cause a homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing, and would typically be visible on imaging, although MRI is indicated if an initial CT is negative. There would not be a pupillary defect.

Sequential occipital cortex infarcts
Sequential occipital cortex infarcts is incorrect. These would also cause a homonymous hemianopia and no pupillary defect.

Tumour recurrence too small to be resolved by CT
Tumour recurrence too small to be resolved by CT is possible, but incorrect. However, in this case the patient has had his right eye irradiated and therefore radiation-induced neuropathy is more likely than tumour recurrence with a negative CT.

stem: A 70-year-old woman presents with sudden loss of vision in one eye. Which one of the following investigations most strongly supports a diagnosis of temporal arteritis?
options: Giant-cell infiltrate in a temporal artery biopsy
explanation:
Giant-cell infiltrate in a temporal artery biopsy
The diagnosis of temporal arteritis is usually made based on clinical history, with markedly raised ESR and CRP, although when there is ambiguity, definitive diagnosis can only be made from the finding of giant-cell infiltrate in a temporal artery biopsy.

Abnormal C-reactive protein
Abnormal C-reactive protein (CRP) is incorrect. Abnormal CRP can be found due to a multitude of causes. In practice, the usefulness of inflammatory markers should be supported by a typical history strongly suggestive of temporal arteritis.

An ESR of 40 mm/h
An ESR of 40 mm/h is incorrect. The range for normal ESR is age dependent = age + 10, divide by 2 for females. In male patients this would be age divided by 2.

Homonymous hemianopia on visual field
Homonymous hemianopia on visual field is incorrect. Homonymous hemianopia can occur as a result of temporal arteritis as this is often a systemic disease, although this would be a rare presentation and would point towards an inflamed artery affecting the posterior visual tract and may be accompanied by other neurological symptoms.

Positive TPHA
Positive TPHA is incorrect. TPHA is a test used to specifically diagnose syphilis.

stem: A 26-year-old man with AIDS is responding well to his initial course of triple therapy. Over the past several months, his CD4 count has improved from less than 50 to 200. He now complains to his genitourinary physician of reduced vision and slight discomfort in his eyes. Which one of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Immune reconstitution uveitis
Immune reconstitution uveitis occurs as a result of the immune system recovering due to effective antiretroviral therapy. As the CD4 count rises, an inflammatory response can develop, leading to uveitis, which is an inflammation of the uvea. Symptoms often include eye discomfort and vision changes, which match the patient's complaints. The autoimmune mechanisms involved in immune reconstitution uveitis are welldocumented in patients experiencing significant immune recovery.

Toxoplasmosis
Toxoplasmosis can cause reduced vision in individuals with HIV but it is typically associated with very low CD4 counts, often less than 100 cells/mm 3. The patient's improved CD4 count to 200 makes this diagnosis less likely. Additionally, toxoplasmosis often presents with focal neurological deficits and retinochoroiditis, which are not described in this case.

Cytomegalovirus retinitis
Cytomegalovirus (CMV) retinitis is incorrect. This condition is a common cause of visual impairment in patients with AIDS but usually occurs when the CD4 count is below 50 cells/mm 3. The patient’s CD4 count has improved significantly to 200, making CMV retinitis less likely. Furthermore, CMV retinitis typically presents with symptoms such as floaters, flashes and a progressive loss of vision, which are not the primary complaints here.

Optic neuritis
While optic neuritis can occur in patients with HIV due to infections like toxoplasmosis, cytomegalovirus and herpes zoster, it is not highly likely in this scenario. Optic neuritis usually presents with more acute vision loss, pain on eye movement and a relative afferent pupillary defect. The patient's symptoms of reduced vision and slight discomfort do not align well with the typical presentation of optic neuritis.

Herpes zoster retinitis
Herpes zoster can cause vision problems in HIV patients, but it is typically associated with very low CD4 counts, often below 100 cells/mm 3. The patient's improved CD4 count to 200 makes this diagnosis less probable. Moreover, herpes zoster retinitis often presents with other signs, such as vesicular skin rashes and severe pain, which are not mentioned in this case.

stem: A 54-year-old man, newly diagnosed with type 2 diabetes mellitus, presents to the Diabetic Screening Clinic for his first assessment. He is found to have changes in his eyes on fundoscopy. Which one of the following is most likely to need urgent referral to the ophthalmologist?
options: Some hard exudates > 1-disc diameter from the fovea
Two cotton-wool spots in the temporal field of the retina
explanation:
New vessels on the disc
New vessels on the disc indicate proliferative diabetic retinopathy, and is graded R3 according to the English National Diabetic Eye Screening Programme grading criteria. They may lead to vitreous haemorrhage and cause loss of vision, and requires urgent assessment by an ophthalmologist.

Cataract
Cataract is incorrect. Diabetes is a risk factor for early development of cataracts. This does not require urgent referral to an ophthalmologist. If the patient has a symptomatic cataract, i.e. is complaining of blurring of vision or night glare, they may be referred to the ophthalmologist on a routine basis.

Microaneurysms
Microaneurysms is incorrect. Microaneurysms reflect background diabetic retinopathy, representing Grade R1 using the screening criteria. This does not need referral to an ophthalmologist. The patient may continue to be monitored by the screening service.

Some hard exudates > 1-disc diameter from the fovea
Some hard exudates > 1-disc diameter from the fovea is incorrect. This patient may have diabetic maculopathy, but does not warrant referral to an ophthalmologist as it is more than one-disc diameter away from the fovea. Referral is required when there are exudates or retinal thickening within one-disc diameter of the fovea, or if there are microaneurysms or haemorrhage within one-disc diameter of the fovea with reduced vision of 6/12 or worse with no other cause found. The patient should thus continue to be monitored by the screening service.

Two cotton-wool spots in the temporal field of the retina.

stem: Which of the following is typically the earliest lesion to develop in diabetic retinopathy?
explanation:
Microaneurysms
The earliest lesions to be detected in diabetic retinopathy are usually capillary microaneurysms.

Blot haemorrhages
Blot haemorrhages is incorrect. Blot haemorrhages, like exudates and venous dilatation, usually appear later.

Hard exudates
Hard exudates is incorrect. Exudates are characteristic of diabetic retinopathy but they, like blot haemorrhages and venous dilatation, usually appear later.

Macular oedema
Macular oedema is incorrect. Macular oedema is a sight-threatening development.

New vessels.

stem: A 49-year-old publican is admitted with confusion and memory loss. His partner tells you he drinks 10-12 pints of beer per day. You suspect he may have Wernicke’s encephalopathy. Which of the following is an eye condition associated with Wernicke’s encephalopathy?
explanation:
Nystagmus
Wernicke's encephalopathy, caused by B1 or thiamine deficiency, is associated with a classic triad of symptoms and signs, namely confusion, ataxia and ophthalmoplegia. Ophthalmoplegia in this case usually affects the lateral rectus muscle. Wernicke’s encephalopathy may also cause nystagmus, which is the most likely finding out of the options given.

Optic neuritis
Optic neuritis is incorrect. This is a demyelinating inflammation of the optic nerve, which is most commonly associated with multiple sclerosis. It is not a known complication of Wernike's encephalopathy.

Miosis
Miosis is incorrect. This is not a sign associated with Wernicke’s encephalopathy. There are a range of causes for miosis, including physiological, pharmacological and pathological causes.

Mydriasis
Mydriasis is incorrect. This is not a sign associated with Wernicke’s encephalopathy. Mydriasis may be caused by damage to the parasympathetic pathway, or may be physiological or pharmacologically induced.

Paralysis of upward gaze
Paralysis of upward gaze is incorrect. A lesion of the vertical gaze pathways may be caused by multiple conditions or factors, including progressive supranuclear palsy. It is not commonly associated with Wernicke’s encephalopathy.

stem: A patient is being referred to the eye clinic with suspected early diabetic retinopathy. Which one of the following tests, if abnormal, most strongly supports the diagnosis?
explanation:
Fluorescein angiography
The earliest sign of diabetic retinopathy is the presence of micro-aneurysms. This is usually a clinical diagnosis with a simple fundal examination and/or fundal photographs. However, of the above options, micro-aneurysms may be seen clearly on fluorescein angiography as small areas of leakage.

Electroretinography
Electroretinography (ERG) is incorrect. Electroretinography is not classically performed in any stage of diabetic retinopathy, as the diagnosis may be made clinically with or without fluorescein angiography. It would be unlikely to add any value unless there is doubt regarding the cause of retinal findings.

B-scan ultrasound
B-scan ultrasound is incorrect. B-scan ultrasound is particularly useful in examining the vitreous and the vitreoretinal interface. It is not used to diagnose diabetic retinopathy. It is typically used in diabetic patients in the presence of vitreous haemorrhage, to exclude a retinal detachment, but would not be used to identify microaneurysms and early diabetic changes.

Visual evoked potentials (VEP)
Visual evoked potentials (VEP) is incorrect. This test measures the electrical signal over the occipital cortex in response to a light stimulus, evaluating the afferent visual pathway. It is typically used to diagnose optic nerve dysfunction, demyelination and albinism. It has no role in the diagnosis of diabetic retinopathy.

Intraocular pressure.

stem: A 60-year-old diabetic complains of floaters of 24 hours’ duration, followed by sudden painless loss of vision in his right eye. His corrected visual acuities are 6/60 (right eye) and 6/12 (left eye). His right retina cannot be visualised, and the left retina contains scattered pigmented spots in the periphery. What is the most appropriate management plan?
options: Admit for laser treatment within 48 hours
Ophthalmology review in the Emergency Department
explanation:
Ophthalmology review in the Emergency Department
The likely cause of reduced vision in this case is a vitreous haemorrhage. Proliferative diabetic retinopathy results in abnormal, fragile new blood vessels growing into the vitreous from the retina, as a result of ischaemia. These abnormal vessels can bleed. If small, the bleed can be asymptomatic, or cause floaters. If more severe, this causes sudden painless loss of vision. The haemorrhage in the vitreous cavity obscures the patient’s view out of the eye and the doctor’s view of the retina. Specialist review is advised to triage the patient with respect to further management.

Stop daily aspirin
Stop daily aspirin is incorrect. Aspirin makes no difference to the duration or severity of a vitreous haemorrhage.

Admit for laser treatment within 48 hours
Admit for laser treatment within 48 hours is incorrect. Laser treatment is required in the form of panretinal photocoagulation to induce regression of the new blood vessels, which have to be presumed to be the cause of the haemorrhage. The pigmented spots in the other eye are probably old laser scars from previous treatment of proliferative diabetic retinopathy. However, laser treatment does not need to be instituted within 48 hours– it should be delayed until the haemorrhage spontaneously clears enough to allow a sufficient view of the retina to permit the application of laser burns. This might occur days or weeks later.

Prescribe oral acetazolamide
Prescribe oral acetazolamide is incorrect. A central retinal artery occlusion does cause sudden painless loss of vision, and is more common in ‘vasculopaths’, but there would be a clear view of the retina and the characteristic cherry red spot in the macula, due to retinal oedema around the fovea. Various measures have been suggested for managing central retinal artery occlusion, including rebreathing of carbon dioxide and sudden lowering of intraocular pressure to try to dislodge the embolus, either medically (acetazolamide) or by anterior chamber paracentesis. Diabetic Retinopathy A teenager is referred by his optometrist with a diagnosis of Lisch nodules of the iris.

Admit for retinal reattachment surgery
Admit for retinal reattachment surgery is incorrect. A retinal detachment could be the cause of his symptoms, and ultrasound of the eye might confirm this. However, this is less likely than vitreous haemorrhage to be the cause of vision loss in a diabetic patient, and rest overnight would allow the haemorrhage to settle enough to view the retina directly, depending on how dense the haemorrhage is, and on whether there is rebleeding.

stem: A 72-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department with a one-week history of double vision when looking to the right. When she looks straight at you the right eye appears deviated medially. Apart from a mild headache at the onset of her symptoms, she otherwise feels well. Past medical history includes controlled hypertension and hypercholesterolaemia. She is a non-smoker. Ocular movements demonstrate a failure of the right eye to abduct beyond the midline and confirm symptomatic diplopia when looking to the right. All other movements appear normal, and a full neurological examination reveals no further abnormality. Pupil reactions are normal. There is no ptosis. Visual acuities are normal. Cardiovascular examination is normal, with a blood pressure of 124/86 mmHg. Which one of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Isolated right sixth nerve palsy
Failure of abduction of the right eye is consistent with a lateral rectus palsy. There are no other neurological deficits mentioned in the scenario, suggesting an isolated sixth nerve palsy. This is commonly caused by microvascular disease, with diabetes, hypertension and hyperlipidaemia known risk factors. The patient should be followed up to ensure resolution over 6–12 weeks. If there is no improvement, neuroimaging is advised to exclude compressive causes.

Duane syndrome
Duane syndrome is incorrect. Duane syndrome is a congenital condition and thus commonly presents in childhood. Acute onset of double vision, as in this adult patient, is not suggestive of Duane syndrome. There is failure of abduction of the affected eye, with retraction of the globe on adduction and narrowing of the palpebral fissure. Adduction may also be affected in type 2 or 3 Duane syndrome.

Myasthenia gravis
Myasthenia gravis is incorrect. Myasthenia gravis may manifest as a sixth nerve palsy, and should be considered as a differential diagnosis. However, there is usually ptosis which is not present here. In view of the patient’s microvascular risk factors and absence of other neurological deficits, an isolated sixth nerve palsy is more likely.

Thyroid eye disease
Thyroid eye disease is incorrect. This may cause restriction of movement of extra-ocular muscles. However, the inferior rectus is more commonly affected with restricted upgaze.

Cerebral infarct
Cerebral infarct is incorrect. There are no other neurological deficits, which makes the diagnosis of a cerebral infarct less plausible as a sixth nerve palsy is unlikely to occur in isolation.

stem: A 70-year-old woman with a history of rheumatoid arthritis comes to the Emergency Department with sudden, painful loss of vision in her left eye. She has a history of hypertension, which is managed with ramipril 10 mg daily and amlodipine 5 mg, and she has type 2 diabetes, which is controlled with metformin. She is taking hydroxychloroquine for her rheumatoid arthritis, aspirin over the counter for intermittent headache and amitriptyline for depression. On examination her BP is 152/92 mmHg; there is increased intraocular pressure, more marked in the left eye than the right; fundoscopy is difficult due to the likely presence of inflammation; both pupils look partially dilated. Which one of the following drugs is the most likely cause of these problems?
explanation:
Amitriptyline
Drugs that cause acute closed-angle glaucoma include tricyclic antidepressants (including amitriptyline), antihistamines, anti-parkinsonian agents, antipsychotics and sulphonamides. Treatment involves a combination of acetazolamide, ß-blocking eye drops, -adrenergic eye drops and pilocarpine. The causative medication should be stopped, although around one third of patients require permanent therapy to lower the intraocular pressure despite discontinuing the responsible medicine. α

Hydroxychloroquine
Hydroxychloroquine is incorrect. Chronic toxicity mimics open-angle glaucoma.

Metformin
Metformin is incorrect. This is associated with B 12 deficiency, which could contribute to a toxic optic neuropathy.

Aspirin
Aspirin is incorrect. This has no significant association with glaucoma.

Ramipril
Ramipril is incorrect. Administration at night can increase nocturnal hypotension, which can worsen glaucoma.

stem: A 74-year-old man is treated with Dorzolamide eye drops for glaucoma. Which of the following correctly reflects the mode of action of Dorzolamide?
explanation:
Carbonic anhydrase inhibitor
Dorzolamide is carbonic anhydrase inhibitor, which leads to a reduction in aqueous production thus reducing intraocular pressure. Prostaglandin analogues such as latanoprost are first-line in the treatment of open angle glaucoma, however carbonic anhydrase inhibitors may be a useful additional or alternative treatment.

Alpha-blocker
Alpha-blocker is incorrect. Alpha-blockers are not used in the treatment of glaucoma. Alpha-2 agonists may be used, usually as a fourth-line treatment, as they are usually not well tolerated due to their side effects of allergy and red eye. They reduce aqueous production and increase uveoscleral flow. Examples include brimonidine and apraclonidine.

Beta-blocker
Beta-blocker is incorrect. Beta-blockers are often used in the treatment of open angle glaucoma, although they are not advised in normal tension glaucoma. Examples include timolol and levobunolol. These reduce aqueous production.

Hyperosmotic
Hyperosmotic is incorrect. This includes agents such as mannitol or glycerol, administered intravenously or orally respectively. This is rarely used due to potential serious adverse effects, including electrolyte imbalance, pulmonary congestion, disorientation and kidney disease.

Parasympathomimetic
Parasympathomimetic is incorrect. Pilocarpine, a parasympathomimetic, works by increasing aqueous drainage or outflow, thus reducing intraocular pressure. It is not commonly used as long-term management, but has benefits in the management of acute angle closure glaucoma.

stem: A 32-year-old woman presents as an emergency with sudden, painless loss of vision in her right eye. She has been a type 1 diabetic for the past 16 years. On examination, her vision is reduced to hand movements in the right eye. Pupil reactions are normal. Dilated fundal examination reveals a vitreous haemorrhage with limited fundal view. Which of the following would be the most likely causative retinal abnormality?
explanation:
Neovascularisation at the optic disc
Neovascularisation is a feature of proliferative diabetic retinopathy, and may occur at the optic disc or elsewhere along the vascular arcades. Neovascularisation can lead to vitreous haemorrhage, which can take several weeks to self-resolve. The patient requires urgent panretinal photocoagulation once fundal view is sufficient.

Microaneurysm
Micro-aneurysm is incorrect. Micro-aneurysms are a feature of mild diabetic retinopathy. They would not cause a deterioration in visual acuity to hand movements.

Cotton-wool spot
Cotton-wool spot is incorrect. Cotton-wool spots are a feature of diabetic and hypertensive retinopathy, signifying ischaemia of the retinal ganglion cells. They would not cause such deterioration of vision.

Hard exudates
Hard exudates is incorrect. Hard exudates in the fundi may occur in diabetic and hypertensive retinopathy. They may also occur in the macula as a feature of diabetic maculopathy. However, they would not cause an abrupt loss of vision as seen in this patient.

Venous beading
Venous beading is incorrect. Venous beading is a feature of diabetic retinopathy, and may occur in other microvascular conditions. Venous beading alone will not lead to profound visual loss.

stem: A 30-year-old patient presents with a 1-day history of monocular visual loss on the right associated with pain behind the eye and alteration of colour vision. Examination the following day reveals a relative afferent pupillary defect in the right eye. Which of the following diagnoses is most likely?
explanation:
Optic neuritis
The history is suggestive of an acute optic nerve lesion. The associated pain and young age of the patient make optic neuritis the most likely diagnosis.

Cerebral infarction
Cerebral infarction is incorrect. Cerebral infarction typically causes a homonymous hemianopia or quadrantanopia.

Migraine
Migraine is incorrect. Migraine can cause monocular disturbances, but these are usually in the form of spreading visual disturbance lasting minutes, in the context of headache. A relative afferent pupillary defect would not be seen.

Optic nerve glioma
Optic nerve glioma is incorrect. Optic nerve glioma usually presents over a longer period.

Temporal arteritis
Temporal arteritis can cause acute optic neuropathy (ischaemic), but does not occur in patients < 50 years of age.

stem: A 26-year-old man presents with sudden-onset headache and double vision. The doctor in the Emergency Department diagnoses a IIIrd (oculomotor) nerve palsy and notes a dilated pupil on that side. Which one of the following is the most likely cause?
explanation:
Posterior communicating artery aneurysm
The IIIrd (oculomotor) nerve emerges in the interpeduncular fossa, passes between the posterior cerebral and superior cerebellar arteries and pierces the dura at the lateral clinoid process to enter the lateral wall of the cavernous sinus. Causes of palsy include: Posterior communicating artery aneurysm – sometimes associated with headache and usually involving pupillary fibres causing an ipsilateral dilated pupil Patients with a new onset, pupil-involving, isolated oculomotor nerve palsy require urgent investigation for an aneurysm which may require urgent treatment to prevent sub-arachnoid haemorrhage

Acoustic neuroma
Acoustic neuroma is incorrect. An acoustic neuroma does not typically affect the oculomotor nerve given its location.

Diabetes mellitus
Diabetes mellitus is incorrect. Diabetes mellitus causes a microvascular infarct of the nerve, and is more commonly painless and associated with sparing of the pupillomotor fibres.

Extradural haematoma
Extradural haematoma is incorrect. Palsy can be caused by pressure on the nerve in ‘coning’ – this however develops gradually and other neurological signs are often present. Oculomotor Nerve (cranial nerve III) Palsy

Ophthalmoplegic migraine
Ophthalmoplegic migraine is incorrect. Ophthalmoplegic migraine is a much less common cause of a painful IIIrd nerve palsy and should be a diagnosis of exclusion.

stem: A 60-year-old man presents with episodic loss of vision in his right eye due to carotid stenosis. He is quite clear that during these episodes the vision in his left eye is normal as he has tested this by closing each eye in turn. What is the most likely pattern of visual field loss?
explanation:
Uniocular altitudinal loss
A monocular disturbance must lie in the retinal or optic nerve circulation, which is arranged into upper and lower main divisions. Disturbances produce either total, arcuate or altitudinal visual field loss.

Bitemporal hemianopia
Bitemporal hemianopia is incorrect. A bitemporal hemianopia is due to chiasmal pathology, most commonly a pituitary tumour; this would typically cause constant and bilateral symptoms.

Homonymous hemianopia
Homonymous hemianopia is incorrect. If the disturbance was bilateral then he might have had a homonymous hemianopia due to a transient ischaemic attack.

Enlarged physiological blind spot
Enlarged physiological blind spot is incorrect. An enlarged blind spot may arise from optic disc swelling, typically from papilloedema; this is usually bilateral.

Bilateral central scotoma
Bilateral central scotomas is incorrect. Bilateral central scotomas would, by definition, affect both eyes.

stem: A 42-year-old woman was seen in the Emergency Department. She complains of an acutely painful and gritty right eye. On examination, she has normal visual acuity. Which diagnosis should prompt an immediate same-day review by Ophthalmology?
explanation:
Contact lens-related ulcer
A patient should be assessed immediately by an Ophthalmologist if they have a suspected serious and potentially sight-threatening, cause of red eye. Causes include acute glaucoma, corneal laceration, contact lensrelated ulcer, corneal ulcer, endophthalmitis, intraocular foreign body, trauma or chemical injury.

Episcleritis
Episcleritis causes mild pain and redness. Patients should be reassured that the condition is usually self-limiting and not dangerous. Oral non-steroidal anti-inflammatories and artificial tears may help relieve discomfort.

Infective conjunctivitis
Adenoviruses are the most common cause of infective conjunctivitis. It is difficult to differentiate between viral and bacterial infections clinically. Swabs should not be taken routinely, and discussion with Ophthalmology should be considered if there is diagnostic difficulty or if there are red flag signs for a serious cause of red eye.

Subconjunctival haemorrhage
Subconjunctival haemorrhage should be managed conservatively, with reassurance that the condition will clear within two weeks. Blood pressure should be checked and coagulopathies/antiplatelet agents should be reviewed.

stem: A 35-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with a two-week history of blurred vision and floaters in his left eye. He is known to be HIV-positive with a CD4 count of 50 cells/μL and has not been on antiretroviral therapy for several months. Ophthalmoscopic examination reveals areas of retinal whitening and haemorrhages along the retinal vessels. What is the most appropriate initial treatment for this condition?
explanation:
Valganciclovir
Valganciclovir is a prodrug of ganciclovir, an oral antiviral medication specifically effective against cytomegalovirus (CMV), which is the causative agent in CMV retinitis, the most likely diagnosis here. In patients with HIV, ganciclovir can significantly reduce viral replication and prevent further damage to the retina, thereby preserving vision. Its use is particularly crucial given that CMV retinitis can progress rapidly if untreated, leading to blindness in affected individuals. Initiating valganciclovir or ganciclovir therapy promptly can help control infection and outcomes.

Acyclovir
Although acyclovir is an antiviral drug used primarily for herpes simplex virus infections, it does not have significant activity against CMV. Therefore, it would not be effective in treating CMV retinitis. Using acyclovir could delay appropriate treatment, allowing the retinitis to worsen and potentially result in irreversible vision loss.

Prednisolone
Prednisolone is a corticosteroid that may be used as an adjunctive treatment in some inflammatory eye conditions but does not target viral infections like CMV retinitis directly. Administering prednisolone without addressing the underlying viral infection could exacerbate immunosuppression and allow unchecked progression of CMV disease.

Rifampicin
Rifampicin is primarily used as part of combination therapy for tuberculosis but has no role in treating viral infections such as CMV retinitis. It lacks efficacy against cytomegalovirus and would, therefore, be inappropriate as an initial treatment for this condition. Neurological and Ophthalmic Disease in Advanced HIVZidovudine
Zidovudine is an antiretroviral medication used to treat HIV by inhibiting HIV's reverse transcriptase; however, it does not have direct activity against cytomegalovirus itself. While important in managing HIV infection overall, zidovudine alone would not adequately address or halt the progression of active CMV retinitis.

stem: A 17-year-old boy presents with sudden blurring of vision affecting his left eye. His past medical history is unremarkable apart from problems with recurrent joint dislocation, shoulder and hip pain. He is doing well at school and is currently planning to sit four A-level exams. On examination he is 6 feet 3 inches in height; his limbs seem abnormally long compared to the size of his body. He has arachnodactyly and pectus excavatum. He tells you he has had a number of teeth removed because of crowding and he has a high-arched palate. Investigations show: haemoglobin 121 g/l, white cell count 4.9 × 10 9/l, platelets 210 × 10 9/l, sodium 137 mmol/l, potassium 4.9 mmol/l and creatinine 100 µmol/l. Ocular examination shows ectopia lentis. Which one of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Marfan’s syndrome
The clinical signs outlined are consistent with Marfan’s syndrome, which is an autosomal dominant disorder caused by mutations of the fibrillin-1 gene on chromosome 15. Ectopia lentis, i.e. a displacement of the lens, may occur in such patients causing visual loss. They are also at risk of aortic dilatation, mitral valve abnormalities, corneal abnormalities and retinal detachment.

Stickler’s syndrome
Stickler’s syndrome is incorrect. Patients with Stickler’s syndrome may have hypermobile joints, however they usually have other characteristic features not mentioned in the scenario. These include a flattened facial appearance, cleft palate and micrognathia. Ocular involvement may occur with high myopia, retinal detachment, cataracts and glaucoma. Ectopia lentis is not a typical occurrence in these patients.

Ehler's Danlos syndrome
Ehlers-Danlos syndrome is incorrect. Ehlers-Danlos syndrome is a rare cause of ectopia lentis, although joint hypermobility is more typical. However, clinical features such as tall stature, arachnodactyly and a high-arched palate are much more suggestive of Marfan’s syndrome.

Homocystinuria
Homocystinuria is incorrect. Whilst patients with homocystinuria share many of the same clinical features as Marfan’s syndrome, they usually suffer with thromboembolic events, such as retinal vein or artery occlusion. Additionally, they typically have a degree of learning disability. Lens DislocationA 54-year-old man with a history of Type 1 diabetes and multiple microvascular complications comes to the Emergency Department for review. He is complaining of diplopia which is making it impossible for him to drive. There are no other neurological symptoms. On examination he has an outward deviating right eye and a ptosis; the pupil does not look particularly dilated.

Weil-Marchesani syndrome
Weil-Marchesani syndrome is incorrect. Patients with Weil-Marchesani syndrome typically have a short stature, unlike this patient, although they may also suffer with ectopia lentis.

stem: A 32-year-old woman presents to her GP with a one-week history of decreased vision and pain in her right eye. She was previously fit and well, and has no significant previous ocular or medical history. Examination reveals a visual acuity of 6/60 in the affected eye, with a relative afferent pupil defect. Ocular movements are full but painful. There is red colour desaturation. Fundal examination is normal. The remainder of the neurological examination is normal. Which one of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Retrobulbar optic neuritis
Optic neuritis is characterised by painful eye movements and/or headache, with progressive, unilateral loss of vision over a few days. Colour vision is reduced, with a relative afferent pupillary defect and visual field loss, typically a central scotoma; 50% have optic disc swelling. One should enquire about symptoms of demyelination, including paraesthesiae, transient weakness, double vision, vertigo and bladder dysfunction, to consider multiple sclerosis as the root cause.

Orbital tumour
Orbital tumour is incorrect. This may cause a compressive optic neuropathy, leading to gradual visual loss. This would typically occur over a longer timespan rather than over days.

Non-arteritic anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy
Non-arteritic anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy is incorrect. This typically occurs in males aged 40-60 years of age with vascular risk factors. Optic disc swelling may be sectoral, with flame haemorrhages. All vascular risk factors should be reviewed and optimised, with review at six weeks.

Toxic optic neuropathy
Toxic optic neuropathy is incorrect. This typically occurs bilaterally, with reduced vision occurring over days to weeks. This may occur due to alcohol abuse, smoking, nutritional deficiencies or general malabsorption.

Giant cell arteritis.

stem: A 40-old woman with AIDS presents to the genitourinary clinic with a shadow in her vision in one eye. Which one of the following supports a diagnosis of cytomegalovirus (CMV) retinitis?
explanation:
Vasculitis with haemorrhages
CMV retinitis typically causes sectorial areas of necrotising retinitis with haemorrhages, with a ‘brush-fire’ appearance as it expands towards the periphery. It may occur unilaterally or bilaterally. It is progressive without treatment, and may cause visual loss with macula or optic nerve involvement. Macular oedema and retinal detachment may also manifest. Therapy with oral valganciclovir is the mainstay of treatment.

Conjunctival injection
Conjunctival injection is incorrect. The question specifically asks for a diagnosis of CMV retinitis, implying pathology identified on viewing the retina. Whilst the patient may have conjunctival injection, this is nonspecific and does not support a diagnosis of CMV retinitis.

Mydriasis on the affected side
Mydriasis on the affected side is incorrect. The patient may develop a relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD) on the affected side with optic nerve involvement in CMV. Mydriasis on the affected side, if not physiological or pharmacological, would suggest a defect in the parasympathetic pathway, which would not be consistent with CMV retinitis.

Cells in the anterior chamber
Cells in the anterior chamber is incorrect. Cells in the anterior chamber are not a sign of retinitis, as this is a finding in the anterior chamber. Cells in the anterior chamber are a sign of uveitis or inflammation.

Acute retinal necrosis
Acute retinal necrosis is incorrect. Acute retinal necrosis (ARN) is associated with varicella zoster and herpes simplex viral infections, although it may rarely occur in those with CMV. This appears as white, welldemarcated lesions in the periphery of the retina, and is associated with vitritis and optic nerve swelling. Necrotising vasculitis with haemorrhages is a much more common finding in CMV retinitis.
