The sclera looks normal, there is no discharge and visual acuity bilaterally is 6/6. She is apyrexial and otherwise in good health. Blood tests show.

stem: A 42-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department with sudden, painless vision loss in her left eye. She reports that she woke up this morning unable to see out of her left eye but denies any trauma or previous similar episodes. On examination, her visual acuity is 20/20 in the right eye and counting fingers at one metre in the left eye. A fundoscopic exam reveals a swollen optic disc with haemorrhages. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy
Anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy (AION) typically presents as sudden, painless vision loss, often noticed upon waking. The presence of a swollen optic disc with haemorrhages is characteristic of AION due to ischaemia affecting short posterior ciliary arteries supplying the optic nerve head. Risk factors include hypertension, diabetes mellitus and giant cell arteritis in older patients. Treatment focuses on managing underlying risk factors and preventing further episodes.

Central retinal artery occlusion
Central retinal artery occlusion (CRAO) also presents with sudden, painless vision loss. However, fundoscopic examination usually reveals a pale retina with a cherry-red spot at the macula rather than disc swelling and haemorrhages. CRAO results mostly from embolism or thrombosis affecting retinal arterial circulation rather than affecting optic nerve perfusion only.

Optic neuritis
Optic neuritis often causes painful vision loss. The pain is usually exacerbated by ocular movements and may be accompanied by other neurological symptoms suggestive of multiple sclerosis or other demyelinating diseases. Fundoscopy may show normal findings initially or later reveal pallor if chronic but not acute swelling and haemorrhages like those seen in AION.

Papilloedema
Although papilloedema can present with bilateral swollen optic discs due to raised intracranial pressure, it rarely causes unilateral visual acuity reduction as described here without additional systemic symptoms such as headache or nausea/vomiting indicative of raised intracranial pressure. Optic NeuropathyRetinal detachment
Sudden vision changes can occur in retinal detachment. However, patients commonly report flashes of light or floaters preceding a shadow over their visual field rather than waking up unable to see suddenly without prior warning signs typical for retinal detachment cases found during fundoscopy showing detached retina folds instead.

stem: A 30-year-old man, under investigation for abdominal cramps and passing blood rectally, presents with an acutely painful, red and photophobic eye. What is the most likely sign on ocular examination?
explanation:
Hypopyon
Passing blood rectally is a symptom of inflammatory bowel disease. There are many causes of a red eye but, in this context, iritis (anterior uveitis) should be suspected. The classical symptom of iritis is photophobia. A cardinal sign of iritis is the presence of inflammatory cells in the anterior chamber of the eye, visible with a slit lamp. In cases of severe iritis, the degree of inflammation in the anterior chamber is enough to cause settling of inflammatory cells inferiorly to form a level – a hypopyon. While a hypopyon may imply infective endophthalmitis (eg following cataract surgery), a sterile hypopyon can occur in cases of severe iritis.

Conjunctival purulent discharge
Conjunctival purulent discharge is incorrect. Bacterial conjunctivitis causes purulent discharge but is very unlikely to cause severe pain and photophobia. Iritis does not cause a discharge.

White corneal stromal infiltrate
White corneal stromal infiltrate is incorrect. Microbial keratitis, causing a white corneal infiltrate, is more likely if there is a history of contact lens wear or trauma, such as a corneal abrasion or a corneal foreign body.

Mydriasis of the affected eye
Mydriasis of the affected eye is incorrect. Iritis often causes pupillary miosis, because the pupil becomes adherent to the lens owing to the inflammation. While acute angle closure, an ophthalmological emergency, causes mydriasis in a red, painful eye, it is also less likely in a patient as young as 30.

Swollen optic disc
Swollen optic disc is incorrect. Cerebral metastases from colorectal carcinoma can cause raised intracranial pressure and papilloedema, but this is unlikely in a young patient, and would not cause conjunctival injection (ie a red eye).

stem: A 54-year-old man with a history of Type 1 diabetes and multiple microvascular complications comes to the Emergency Department for review. He is complaining of diplopia which is making it impossible for him to drive. There are no other neurological symptoms. On examination he has an outward deviating right eye and a ptosis; the pupil does not look particularly dilated. Which of the following is the most likely cause?
explanation:
Diabetes mellitus
All of the options listed are potential causes of third nerve palsy. However, the lack of neurological symptoms and signs including headache, pain and pupil dilation supports a microvascular cause such as diabetes mellitus. If the pupil or other cranial nerves were involved, or there was evidence of optic disc swelling, an urgent CT or MRI should be requested. They should be monitored to ensure resolution over 6-12 weeks, with neuroimaging if improvement does not occur.

Giant cell arteritis
Giant cell arteritis is incorrect. There are no symptoms or signs in the scenario to suggest giant cell arteritis, including headache, eye pain, jaw claudication or scalp tenderness. However, this should always be considered as a differential diagnosis, particularly if the patient is over 50 and has no other known microvascular disease. The patient should have an ESR and C-reactive protein blood test.

Idiopathic
Idiopathic is incorrect. This patient may have an idiopathic cause for the third nerve palsy, however in the presence of known microvascular disease, this is not the most likely option.

Posterior communicating artery aneurysm
Posterior communicating artery aneurysm is incorrect. A painful third nerve palsy is suggestive of an aneurysm, and requires emergency neurological referral. This is less likely in the absence of pain and other neurological symptoms, with a known microvascular cause. However, this should always be considered as a cause, with urgent neuroimaging if any doubt remains.

Raised intracranial pressure
Raised intracranial pressure is incorrect. In the absence of neurological symptoms and optic disc swelling, this is less likely to be a cause of the third nerve palsy in this scenario.

stem: A 70-year-old man presents with a gradually worsening, droopy, right upper eyelid. On examination there is a right ptosis and constricted pupil, which appears more pronounced when the room lights are off than in light conditions. He is a heavy smoker who has smoked 20 cigarettes per day for the past 40 years. Which one of the following is the best investigation?
explanation:
Chest X-ray
The signs are consistent with a right Horner syndrome. Horner syndrome has several causes, including Pancoast’s tumour of the lung. Given his history of smoking, that is the most likely diagnosis here. Differential diagnosis of ptosis and anisocoria - A IIIrd nerve palsy would cause ptosis and a fixed dilated pupil. Old age, smoking, elevated blood pressure and diabetes are all risk factors for microvascular ischaemia, which can cause a cranial mononeuropathy (commonly IIIrd and VIth nerve palsies). Additionally, in a IIIrd nerve palsy, the eye is likely to be deviated in the ‘down and out’ position.

Anti-acetylcholine-receptor antibodies
Anti-acetylcholine-receptor antibodies is incorrect. Myasthenia gravis causes a variable ptosis, often bilateral, but never affects the pupils. Therefore, anti-acetylcholine-receptor antibodies would not be the best investigation in the current case.

Blood glucose
Blood glucose is incorrect. In the current case of Horner syndrome, blood glucose would not be the best investigation.

Dilute pilocarpine eye-drop test
Dilute pilocarpine eye-drop test is incorrect. Diluted pilocarpine drops (0.1%) can be used to diagnose a Holmes–Adie pupil. These drops will not constrict a normal pupil, but will constrict a Holmes–Adie pupil due to denervation sensitivity. An Adie pupil, in contrast to Horner’s syndrome, is a dilated pupil, and the anisocoria is more noticeable in brighter conditions.

Intraocular pressure
Intraocular pressure is incorrect. Elevated intraocular pressure in acute angle closure causes pupillary dilation in a red, painful eye, but ptosis does not occur, although pain in the eye can cause intermittent blepharospasm. Intraocular pressure is unaffected in Horner’s syndrome.

stem: A 32-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis presents to the Rheumatology Clinic with a complaint of severe pain and reduced vision in one of her eyes. The medical specialist trainee notes that one eye is dusky red in colour and that the vision in this eye is reduced to 6/36. What is the appropriate management?
options: The patient should be booked for an urgent CT scan
The patient should be investigated urgently for coexisting inflammatory bowel disease
The patient should be started immediately on systemic immunosuppressant therapy
The patient should be started on artificial tears
The patient should be referred urgently to the ophthalmology clinic
explanation:
The patient should be referred urgently to the ophthalmology clinic
A red painful eye in an individual with a history of connective tissue disease should be referred urgently to the Ophthalmology Clinic for urgent diagnosis and treatment. Scleritis and uveitis are diagnoses that must be ruled out and treated promptly for visual preservation. Often they are started on artificial tears or antibiotics as empiric treatment, which offer no benefit. Further along in their management they may be investigated for other coexisting inflammatory diseases.

The patient should be booked for an urgent CT scan
The patient should be booked for an urgent CT scan is incorrect. CT scan is unnecessary at the first instance, unless advised by the ophthalmologists following a full ocular examination.

The patient should be investigated urgently for coexisting inflammatory bowel disease
The patient should be investigated urgently for coexisting inflammatory bowel disease is incorrect. This is unnecessary unless the patient complains specifically of associated gastrointestinal symptoms. Even so, it is not usually an ‘urgent’ investigation.

The patient should be started immediately on systemic immunosuppressant therapy
The patient should be started immediately on immunosuppressant therapy is incorrect. Systemic immunosuppressant therapy is unnecessary at the first instance, unless advised by the ophthalmologist following full ocular examination and failure for ocular disease control with topical therapy.

The patient should be started on artificial tears
The patient should be started on artificial tears is incorrect. Artificial tears while used as an empiric treatment rarely offer benefit.

stem: A 48-year-old Caucasian male presents to his optometrist with a one-month history of blurred vision in his left eye. Visual acuity is 6/12 in the affected eye, 6/6 in the right eye. Fundal examination reveals some mottled pigmentary changes at the left macula, associated with some macular oedema. On closer inspection, both fundi reveal reddish-brown bands deep to the retina radiating in a spoke-like pattern from the optic disc. The optician referred the patient to his GP, who noted loose skin folds with yellow striations and puckering in the neck and flexor aspects of the joints. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Pseudoxanthoma elasticum
Pseudoxanthoma elasticum is an inherited disorder characterised by progressive calcification of elastic fibres, primarily affecting the eye, skin and cardiovascular system. Initially, it may manifest with a ‘peau d’orange’ appearance before progressing to angioid streaks, as described in this scenario as bands radiating in a spokelike pattern. Angioid streaks, caused by breaks in Bruch’s membrane, do not affect vision by themselves, but choroidal neovascularisation may occur as a complication with subsequent reduced visual acuity and distortion. These may be idiopathic or part of a systemic disorder. The skin changes of loose skin folds and puckering is consistent with cutaneous features of pseudoxanthoma elasticum, also referred to as the ‘plucked chicken’ appearance.

Ehlers-Danlos syndrome
Ehlers?Danlos syndrome is incorrect. Ehlers?Danlos syndrome is another systemic association of angioid streaks, and causes hypermobility of joints and hyperelasticity. This should be considered as a differential diagnosis, although the puckering appearance described is characteristic of pseudoxanthoma elasticum.

Paget’s disease
Paget’s disease is incorrect. This is usually associated with the elderly, and is another cause of angioid streaks.

Marfan syndrome
Marfan syndrome is incorrect. Typical characteristics of Marfan syndrome, such as hypermobile joints, higharched palate and tall stature, are not mentioned here. The cutaneous changes described in the scenario are also not consistent with Marfan syndrome, although angioid streaks may feature.

Sickle cell disease
Sickle cell disease is incorrect. This is a less likely diagnosis in a Caucasian gentleman. There are no supporting systemic features of sickle cell disease in the scenario.

stem: A 21-year-old man is sent to the Ophthalmology Clinic for review. He is keen to become a pilot, but was referred after failing his pre-flight training medical on grounds of myopia and severely restricted peripheral visual fields. He is otherwise completely well with no other significant past medical history of note and he takes no medication. On examination both retina show arteriolar attenuation and pigmented bone-spicules in the mid-periphery, with pallor of the optic disc. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Retinitis pigmentosa
The fundus findings described are typical of that seen in retinitis pigmentosa, a hereditary condition which causes progressive rod dysfunction. Symptoms include gradual loss of night and peripheral vision. Central vision is usually preserved until disease is very advanced. Family members should be examined to determine the mode of inheritance, which is autosomal recessive in 60% of cases. This may be performed in conjunction with genetic testing. The patient should undergo electroretinography to confirm rod dysfunction. At present there is no definitive treatment although gene therapy trials are in progress. Counselling, low vision aids and support groups should be offered to the patient. Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors may be useful in the presence of macular oedema.

Glaucoma
Glaucoma is incorrect. Whilst this should be a differential when considering causes of visual field loss and optic disc pallor, the bone-spicule appearance is not consistent with glaucoma. The scenario does not mention any risk factors for glaucoma to present in a 21-year-old.

Choroideremia
Choroideremia is incorrect. This is also a hereditary condition (X-linked) and causes visual field loss and night blindness in young males. Irregular fundal pigmentation may occur, similar to retinitis pigmentosa. However, in choroideremia, there is less attenuation of retinal blood vessels and absence of the typical bone-spicule appearance. Choroideremia causes RPE and choriocapillaris atrophy in the mid-periphery with visible choroidal vessels and sclera.

Stargadt’s disease
Stargadt’s disease is incorrect. This is an autosomal recessive condition causing macula disease and cone dysfunction, not rod dysfunction as seen in retinitis pigmentosa. Whilst similar pigmentation may occur in the fundus, peripheral visual fields are full, with progressive loss of central vision.

Usher’s syndrome
Usher’s syndrome is incorrect. Usher’s syndrome is a systemic disorder associated with retinitis pigmentosa. However, patients with Usher’s syndrome will experience neurosensory hearing loss, which is not mentioned in this scenario. Type 1 and Type 2 Usher’s syndrome cause deafness in childhood, whilst Type 3 causes progressive hearing loss in adulthood.

stem: An 82-year-old woman presents with sudden loss of vision in her left eye. On further questioning, she complains of a left-sided headache over the past few weeks, associated with tenderness of her head when she brushes her hair. On examination, her vision is reduced to counting fingers in the left eye. A left relative afferent pupillary defect is present. Fundoscopy reveals a pale, swollen left optic disc with some flame-shaped haemorrhages. The right eye is entirely normal. An urgent erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) is elevated at 72 mm/h. Which one of the following management options should be carried out first?
options: Computed tomography (CT) scan of brain and orbits
explanation:
Administration of high-dose systemic steroids
The symptoms and signs, coupled with an elevated ESR, are consistent with a diagnosis of giant cell arteritis (GCA) or arteritic ischaemic optic neuropathy (AION). GCA should always be suspected in a patient over the age of 50 who presents with a history of headache and scalp tenderness. Other systemic symptoms include scalp tenderness, jaw claudication, weight loss and fever. It is associated with polymyalgia rheumatica. ESR and Creactive protein are typically raised, and ocular examination reveals a relative afferent pupillary defect, optic disc swelling and impaired colour vision. To avoid visual loss in the contralateral eye, high-dose systemic steroids should be commenced immediately.

Temporal artery biopsy
Temporal artery biopsy is incorrect. If a diagnosis of GCA is suspected clinically, steroids may be commenced without first performing a temporal artery biopsy. A biopsy should typically be performed within the first two weeks following the onset of symptoms, but a relatively high false-negative rate is likely due to the presence of skip lesions.

Ophthalmic outpatient review
Ophthalmic outpatient review is incorrect. Once GCA is suspected, patients may be admitted for intravenous steroids or commenced on high-dose oral steroids and seen daily as an outpatient. This should be arranged after steroids have been started.

Automated visual field assessment
Automated visual field assessment is incorrect. This may be performed after commencing steroids and to monitor progress, but is not the most immediate management step in the acute setting of GCA.

Computed tomography (CT) scan of brain and orbits
Computed tomography (CT) scan of brain and orbits is incorrect. This patient has clinical features of GCA and thus should be treated as such; however, if there is any doubt regarding the diagnosis, a CT scan may be performed to exclude a compressive optic nerve tumour causing optic neuropathy. Visual loss in this case is usually gradual and progressive, without the systemic features of GCA.

stem: A 28-year-old Afro-Caribbean man presents with a three-week history of painful, red eyes associated with floaters and sensitivity to light. He also complains of pain in several of his joints. Ocular examination reveals evidence of bilateral posterior uveitis. On systemic examination, tender nodules can be palpated over both shins. Serum ACE is positive. Which one of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Sarcoidosis
Sarcoidosis is a multi-system granulomatous disease characterised by chronic non-caseating granuloma formation. It typically affects individuals of Afro-Caribbean origin aged between 20 and 50 years. Systemic manifestations mentioned in the above scenario include arthritis and erythema nodosum. Bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy, pulmonary infiltrates and skin lesions may also be present. Sarcoidosis can present primarily with ocular involvement, namely posterior uveitis, optic nerve involvement, cataract, glaucoma or venous occlusion.

Tuberculosis (TB)
Tuberculosis (TB) is incorrect. This should form part of the differential diagnoses when considering causes of systemic disease and posterior uveitis. However, the scenario mentions a positive serum ACE consistent with sarcoidosis. A patient with this presentation should undergo testing for both conditions, particularly as steroid treatment may reactivate TB.

Behcet’s disease
Behcet’s disease is incorrect. This is a systemic disorder most commonly affecting young men of Mediterranean origin. It commonly causes recurrent mouth and genital ulcers, erythema nodosum and a chronic uveitis. An ischaemic vasculitis may occur, affecting both arteries and veins.

Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada syndrome
Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada syndrome is incorrect. This is a systemic condition with cutaneous and ocular involvement, occurring most commonly in Japanese, Hispanic and Asian populations. However, it usually causes anterior uveitis with or without a serous retinal detachment, choroiditis and optic disc oedema. Cutaneous manifestations include vitiligo, alopecia and poliosis.

stem: A 30-year-old man is referred to the Dermatology Clinic and found to have café au lait spots. Which of the following features subsequently found in the Eye Clinic suggests a diagnosis of neurofibromatosis?
explanation:
Lisch nodules
Lisch nodules are iris nodules, and are the most common clinical sign described in individuals with Neurofibromatosis type 1.

Busacca nodules
Busacca nodules is incorrect. Busacca nodules are seen in ocular sarcoidosis (this is an inflammatory nodule, but the eponym need not be memorised for the MRCP exam).

Brushfield spots
Brushfield spots is incorrect. Brushfield spots are a finding described in people with Down syndrome, although they have also been found in normal individuals.

Koeppe nodules
Koeppe nodules is incorrect. Koeppe nodules are seen in ocular sarcoidosis (this is an inflammatory nodule, but the eponym need not be memorised for the MRCP exam). 823 NeurofibromatosisHeterochromia iridis
Heterochromia iridis is incorrect. Heterochromia iridis is seen in a variety of conditions including congenital Horner’s syndrome, pigment dispersion syndrome, Sturge-Weber syndrome and Waardenburg syndrome.

stem: A diabetic 46-year-old man is found in the Diabetic Clinic to have reduced visual acuity. During a telephone referral to the eye clinic, the ophthalmologist asks whether the patient has any risk factors for macular oedema. Which one of the following should the referring physician bring to his attention?
explanation:
Background diabetic retinopathy
The Wisconsin Epidemiological Study showed that the incidence of macular oedema was 2–6% in background diabetic retinopathy (DR), 20–63% in preproliferative DR and 70–74% in proliferative DR. The prevalence increased with greater duration of diabetes, higher glycosylated haemoglobin and greater proteinuria levels.

Low glycosylated haemoglobin
Low glycated haemoglobin is incorrect. Glycated haemoglobin, also known as HBA1c, is representative of the average plasma glucose concentration over three months and is an indicator of glycaemic control. Low HBA1c is not a risk factor for diabetic maculopathy or macular oedema.

Previous myocardial infarction
Previous myocardial infarction is incorrect. A previous myocardial infarction raises the patient’s cardiovascular profile, but is not considered a direct risk factor for macular oedema.

Recent conjunctivitis
Recent conjunctivitis is incorrect. Conjunctivitis is not a risk factor for macular oedema, although it may have bearing on treatment for macular oedema with anti-vascular endothelial growth factor agents if active.

Peripheral vascular disease
Peripheral vascular disease is incorrect. Peripheral vascular disease is not a risk factor for macular oedema.

stem: A 34-year-old woman presents with a first episode of abrupt visual loss in the left eye. Neuromyelitis optica (NMO), also known as Devic's disease, is diagnosed. Which of the following options is most likely to be effective in treating the acute attack?
options: Methylprednisolone 1 g once daily (OD) intravenously (IV) for 5–7 days
Methyprednisolone 40 mg OD orally (PO) for 5–7 days
Mycophenolate 1 g twice daily (BD) PO for 5–7 days
Cyclophosphamide 1 mg/kg OD PO for 5–7 days
explanation:
Methylprednisolone 1 g once daily (OD) intravenously (IV) for 5–7 days
IV methylprednisolone is a sensible treatment option to limit the inflammation in this instance. The dosing regimen suggested is also that which would be used for a patient with this condition.

Methyprednisolone 40 mg OD orally (PO) for 5–7 days
Oral methylprednisolone is a option to limit the inflammation in neuromyelitis optica. However, the dose suggested is suboptimal and may prove ineffective; ordinarily, 500 mg–2 g of oral methylprednisolone is required.

Plasma exchange for 5–7 days
While there is some evidence from controlled clinical trials that plasma exchange is effective in neuromyelitis optica, this is not a first-line treatment.

Mycophenolate 1 g twice daily (BD) PO for 5–7 days
In neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder (which includes both optic neuritis and transverse myelitis) disabilities may be accumulated from each acute attack including visual problems and/or limb paralysis. Steroid sparing agents (azathioprine, methotrexate or mycophenolate) are used to allow for a reduction of steroids. However, these treatments increase the risk of serious intercurrent infections. Optic Neuritis

Cyclophosphamide 1 mg/kg OD PO for 5–7 days
There is very little evidence for the use of cyclophosphamide in neuromyelitis optica.

stem: A 40-year-old man presents to his GP with unequal pupils. The GP considers that a IIIrd (oculomotor) nerve palsy is the likely diagnosis. Which one of the following statements is true?
options: The pupil on the affected side is smaller
The pupil on the affected side reacts normally to light
The pupil on the contralateral side reacts normally to light shone into the affected eye
The pupil on the affected side reacts normally to accommodation
The pupil size difference is equal in bright and dim surroundings
explanation:
The pupil on the contralateral side reacts normally to light shone into the affected eye
There will be no impairment in the detection of light (IInd or optic nerve) by the eye on the side of the IIIrd nerve palsy, and therefore the contralateral eye’s consensual pupil reaction will be unaffected.

The pupil on the affected side is smaller
The pupil on the affected side is smaller is incorrect. The IIIrd (oculomotor) nerve brings parasympathetic pupillomotor fibres to the iris sphincter – in a palsy, the pupil on the affected side is larger (not smaller).

The pupil on the affected side reacts normally to light
The pupil on the affected side reacts normally to light is incorrect. Light reactions of the pupil on the side of the IIIrd nerve palsy will be impaired, either to a direct (light shone into the ipsilateral eye) or consensual (light shone into the contralateral eye) stimulus. Constriction as part of the near response will also be affected on the side of the IIIrd nerve palsy.

The pupil on the affected side reacts normally to accommodation
The pupil on the affected side reacts normally to accommodation is incorrect. The pupil on the affected side will be unreactive to light or accommodation.

The pupil size difference is equal in bright and dim surroundings.

stem: A physician suspects that his diabetic patient might be at risk of proliferative retinopathy. Which one of the following features on fundoscopy is most likely to lead to proliferative retinopathy?
options: Venous beading in the inferior nasal quadrant
Micro-aneurysms in the superior temporal quadrant
Multiple blot haemorrhages in all four quadrants
explanation:
Multiple blot haemorrhages in all four quadrants
This is consistent with preproliferative or severe non-proliferative diabetic retinopathy, and may lead to neovascularisation. Therefore of the options available, this is the one which is most likely to lead to proliferative retinopathy.

Peripheral cotton-wool spots
Peripheral cotton-wool spots is incorrect. This signifies moderate non-proliferative diabetic retinopathy, with ischaemia of retinal ganglion axons.

Venous beading in the inferior nasal quadrant
Venous beading in the inferior nasal quadrant is incorrect. Venous beading in two quadrants is part of the criteria for diagnosing severe non-proliferative diabetic retinopathy.

Micro-aneurysms in the superior temporal quadrant
Micro-aneurysms in the superior temporal quadrant is incorrect. Micro-aneurysms are consistent with background retinopathy if present in one quadrant. If present in all four quadrants it is consistent with severe non-proliferative diabetic retinopathy.

Peripheral hard exudates
Peripheral hard exudates is incorrect. This is consistent with background retinopathy changes. Classification of non-proliferative diabetic retinopathy (NB: this differs from the diabetic screening service criteria) Mild non-proliferative (background) diabetic retinopathy: at least one micro-aneurysm. Screening criteria includes exudates. Moderate non-proliferative diabetic retinopathy: intra-retinal haemorrhages or micro-aneurysms Severe non-proliferative retinopathy: one of the following: intra-retinal haemorrhages or micro-aneurysms in four quadrants venous beading in two quadrants or more IRMA in one quadrant. Very severe non-proliferative diabetic retinopathy: at least two of the three criteria above. Diabetic Retinopathy A 48-year-old Caucasian male presents to his optometrist with a one-month history of blurred vision in his left eye. Visual acuity is 6/12 in the affected eye, 6/6 in the right eye. Fundal examination reveals some mottled pigmentary changes at the left macula, associated with some macular oedema. On closer inspection, both fundi reveal reddish-brown bands deep to the retina radiating in a spoke-like pattern from the optic disc. The optician referred the patient to his GP, who noted loose skin folds with yellow striations and puckering in the neck and flexor aspects of the joints.

stem: A 68-year-old man presents to his GP with a 24 h history of abrupt loss of vision in his left eye. On examination, his visual acuities are 6/6 in the right eye and 6/60 in the left eye. Dilated fundal examination reveals evidence of widespread retinal haemorrhages in all quadrants of the left retina associated with dilated tortuous retinal veins. The right fundus appears entirely normal. The patient has not seen his GP within the last 10 years. He describes himself as fit and well and is on no regular medication. However, a subsequent examination reveals a blood pressure of 185/100 mmHg and a random blood sugar of 12 mmol/l. Which one of the following is the most likely ocular diagnosis?
explanation:
Central retinal vein occlusion
Sudden, painless and unilateral loss of vision with retinal findings of dilated tortuous retinal veins, plus retinal haemorrhages in all four quadrants, is consistent with central retinal vein occlusion. There may also be cottonwool spots, optic disc swelling, macula oedema and neovascularisation. Risk factors include hypertension, diabetes, hyperlipidaemia and glaucoma. The patient should have a full cardiovascular profile conducted with appropriate optimisation of identified risk factors.

Branch retinal vein occlusion
Branch retinal vein occlusion has the same retinal findings as in central retinal vein occlusion, but they occur in a branched distribution and not in all four quadrants of the retina. It is three times more common than central retinal vein occlusion with similar risk factors.

Hypertensive retinopathy
This patient is hypertensive, but retinal pathology would typically be bilateral. Additionally, signs of hypertensive retinopathy include arteriolar narrowing, arteriovenous nipping and hard exudates. Flame-shaped haemorrhages similar to those seen in central retinal vein occlusion may occur.

Diabetic retinopathy
Similarly, to hypertensive retinopathy, pathology would typically be bilateral. Other retinal findings such as microaneurysms, cotton-wool spots and hard exudates are likely to be present.

Central retinal artery occlusion
Central retinal artery occlusion may also present as painless, abrupt loss of vision in one eye. However, the retina would appear pale due to ischaemia, with a ‘cherry-red spot’ in the macula. There would not be haemorrhages or tortuous retinal veins.

stem: An 80-year-old man is referred to the psychogeriatrician with features of dementia. The neurology Specialist Trainee (ST) confirms that the eye movements are limited in upward gaze on pursuit movements, but that the eyes move upwards normally when he flexes the patient’s neck. The patient is not on any medication. Which of the following conclusions is valid?
options: The patient has an abnormal vestibulo-ocular response
The patient has a supranuclear gaze palsy
The patient has an oculogyric crisis
explanation:
The patient has a supranuclear gaze palsy
The combination of reduced voluntary pursuit movements and maintained vestibulo-ocular response (‘doll’s eye’ movements) is classically seen in supranuclear gaze palsy, where the lesion lies between the cortex and the oculomotor nuclei.

The patient has an abnormal vestibulo-ocular response
The patient has an abnormal vestibulo-ocular response is incorrect. Abnormal vestibulo-ocular response is elicited when there is no preservation of the doll’s eye movement.

The patient has tardive dyskinesia
The patient has tardive dyskinesia is incorrect. Tardive dyskinesia is reported after long term use of antipsychotics and anti-dopaminergic anti-emetics.

The patient has an oculogyric crisis
The patient has an oculogyric crisis is incorrect. Oculogyric crisis is an episode of prolonged involuntary upward movements of both eyes, from the long term use of some medications.

The patient has Korsakoff’s syndrome
The patient has Korsakoff’s syndrome is incorrect. In Korsakoff syndrome we would have expected a history of alcohol abuse, and bilateral rectus palsy and nystagmus are the usual eye signs seen.

stem: A 65-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with a vision defect in his right eye. He reports that his vision has been gradually worsening over the past few weeks, accompanied by dull pain around the eye, and he has also experienced episodes of transient monocular blindness. On examination, there is evidence of neovascularisation on the iris and a relative afferent pupillary defect in the right eye. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Ocular ischaemic syndrome
Ocular ischaemic syndrome (OIS) typically presents with symptoms such as gradual vision loss, amaurosis fugax (transient monocular blindness), and signs like neovascularisation on the iris and a relative afferent pupillary defect. This syndrome results from chronic hypoperfusion to the ocular structures due to severe carotid artery stenosis or occlusion. The gradual worsening of vision over weeks combined with acute episodes strongly suggests an ischemic process rather than an acute event alone. Additionally, neovascularisation on the iris is a commonly encountered feature pointing towards OIS.

Acute angle-closure glaucoma
Acute angle-closure glaucoma typically presents with sudden-onset severe eye pain, headache, nausea, vomiting and blurred vision, along with halos around lights due to increased intraocular pressure. Examination often reveals a mid-dilated pupil that reacts poorly to light along with corneal oedema but not necessarily neovascularisation or relative afferent pupillary defect, which are seen in this case.

Central retinal artery occlusion
Central retinal artery occlusion usually manifests as sudden painless unilateral vision loss associated with a cherry-red spot on fundoscopy but lacks gradual worsening over weeks. It does not commonly present with neovascularisation on the iris. Instead, it shows diffuse retinal whitening.

Giant cell arteritis
Giant cell arteritis often affects individuals above 50 years old, presenting systemic symptoms such as headache, jaw claudication, and scalp tenderness alongside visual symptoms like transient monocular blindness, progressing rapidly if untreated but usually accompanied by elevated inflammatory markers (ESR/CRP). Neovascularisation on the iris is not characteristic nor the slowly progressive visual changes seen here.

Retinal detachment
Retinal detachment typically presents with symptoms such as sudden flashes of light and floaters. It generally does not present with gradual worsening over weeks or transient monocular blindness. The presence of neovascularisation on the iris and relative afferent pupillary defect are not characteristic features of retinal detachment. This condition is usually more acute in onset and lacks the ischemic signs seen in OIS.

stem: A 28-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with a sudden deterioration of vision with severe blurring leading to count fingers vision only in his left eye. Colour vision is intact in both eyes. Visual acuity in the right eye is 6/6. He is tall at 1.92m and thin, with a BMI of 21 kg/m 2. You note that he has pectus excavatum and a long arm span compared to the length of his body. He is hypermobile. Which of the following is the most likely cause of his visual disturbance?
explanation:
Lens dislocation
A number of features consistent with a diagnosis of Marfan’s syndrome or homocystinuria are described in the scenario. Ocular manifestations of Marfan’s syndrome include upward lens dislocation, myopia, corneal abnormalities including keratoconus and retinal detachment. Homocystinuria can present with similar signs, but will present with downward lens dislocation. The most likely cause for his loss of vision in the above options is lens dislocation.

Glaucoma
Glaucoma is incorrect. Sudden deterioration of vision may occur in acute angle closure glaucoma, however this is painful and associated with headache and nausea. This patient is also relatively young to have glaucoma.

Optic neuritis
Optic neuritis is incorrect. This typically causes painful eye movements, which is not mentioned in the above scenario. It is also not an associated finding with Marfan’s syndrome.

Cataract
Cataract is incorrect. A cataract would not cause an abrupt loss of vision. It typically causes gradual loss of vision and is usually bilateral. Lens DislocationA 54-year-old man, newly diagnosed with type 2 diabetes mellitus, presents to the Diabetic Screening Clinic for his first assessment. He is found to have changes in his eyes on fundoscopy. Which one of the following is most likely to need urgent referral to the ophthalmologist?

Retinal vein occlusion
Retinal vein occlusion is incorrect. Fundal examination should be performed in any patient with acute loss of vision. Retinal vein occlusion is a cause of painless loss of vision, however it is not commonly associated with Marfan’s syndrome, which is a connective tissue disorder.

stem: A 19-year-old man with Ehlers-Danlos Type IV comes to the Emergency Department because of acute painless loss of vision in his right eye. He had normal vision (6/6) in both eyes until he awoke on the morning of presentation, where his vision had deteriorated to count fingers. Examination of the left eye is normal. Anterior segment examination of the right eye was normal. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Retinal detachment
The above options are all possible manifestations of Ehlers-Danlos syndrome. Patients are typically myopic (short-sighted), with increased risk of retinal detachment. This requires urgent surgical repair.

Lens dislocation
Lens dislocation is incorrect. This may also cause a painless reduction in visual acuity if lens subluxation occurs. However, we are told that the anterior segment examination is normal.

Cataract
Cataract is incorrect. This would not cause an abrupt loss of vision from 6/6 to count fingers. Cataracts typically cause a gradual progressive loss of vision, and is usually bilateral.

Macular degeneration
Macular degeneration is incorrect. This would not occur in a 19-year-old male, as it is an age-related disorder commonly seen in the elderly. This would also cause a gradual loss of vision.

Keratoconus
Keratoconus is incorrect. This may cause reduction in visual acuity with progressive irregular astigmatism. This would not cause such an abrupt loss of vision.

stem: Which of the following examination findings is most likely to be present?
explanation:
Kayser–Fleischer rings
This patient has liver impairment. The only sign listed here associated with liver impairment is Kayser–Fleischer rings, which can be found in Wilson’s disease, an autosomal recessive condition secondary to excess copper deposition. The disease presents with features of hepatitis and neuropsychiatric symptoms such as depression, dementia and chorea. Kayser–Fleischer rings are green/brown in colour and appear to encircle the iris, secondary to copper deposition in Descemet’s membrane of the cornea.

Band keratopathy
Band keratopathy is due to calcium deposition in chronic eye disease or due to hypercalcaemia.

Cornea verticillata
Cornea verticillata (vortex keratopathy) is a common side effect of amiodarone (and rarely due to chloroquine, hydroxychloroquine, indometacin, tamoxifen, chlorpromazine or Fabry’s disease).

Corneal arcus
Corneal arcus is a common finding in the elderly population and can be related to hyperlipidaemia.

Hudson–Stahli lines.

stem: A patient presents to Medical Outpatients with diplopia. Which one of the following suggests that the IVth cranial nerve (the trochlear nerve) is involved?
options: The diplopia is worse at night
The diplopia is worse for distance- than near-vision
explanation:
The diplopia is torsional
The trochlear nerve (IVth cranial nerve) supplies the superior oblique muscle, which depresses the eye and rotates it inwardly. Lesions of this nerve cause outward rotation and a torsional element to the diplopia.

The diplopia is horizontal
The diplopia is horizontal is incorrect. Horizontal diplopia occurs when the recti muscles for horizontal eye movements fail to move in a conjugate manner. This would refer to interruptions to the medial or lateral recti in either eye.

The diplopia is episodic
The diplopia is episodic is incorrect. Intermittent and episodic episodes of diplopia refers to fluctuations in the control of conjugated eye movements in any direction, and is not specific to the IVth cranial nerve. Myasthenia gravis, thyroid eye disease, multiple sclerosis and squint decompensation should be suspected.

The diplopia is worse at night
The diplopia is worse at night is incorrect. Diplopia that gets worse during the day illustrates eye movement control that wanes with time. Myasthenia gravis should be excluded. 830 Trochlear Nerve (Cranial Nerve IV) PalsyThe diplopia is worse for distance- than near-vision
The diplopia is worse for distance- than near-vision is incorrect. Diplopia worse at distance suggests divergence insufficiency which is a benign phenomenon and usually resolves spontaneously. However bilateral VIth cranial nerve palsy should be considered. Neuroimaging may be useful to exclude mass lesions and demyelinating disease in non-resolving cases with other sinister symptoms.

stem: A 78-year-old woman attends the Emergency Department with a sudden loss of vision in her left eye. She mentions that she has been suffering from headaches, anorexia and arthralgias for about 2 months. These symptoms have been partly relieved by non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs. One month ago she tripped while out and banged her head on a park bench. She did not see a doctor on that occasion. There is no past medical history of note. What is the most likely cause of her visual loss?
explanation:
Arteritic ischaemic optic neuritis
This woman has giant-cell arteritis with consequent ischaemic optic neuritis until proven otherwise. Other features that might be helpful in the history are headaches, temporal tenderness (over the temporal arteries), loss of temporal artery pulse and pain in the jaw on chewing (jaw claudication). The visual loss in the affected eye is often irreversible, and the second eye is at immediate risk. This condition therefore requires urgent treatment with corticosteroids.

Demyelinating optic neuritis
Demyelinating optic neuritis is incorrect. Demyelinating optic neuritis is unusual in this age group and does not usually produce such sudden visual loss.

Migraine
Migraine is incorrect. Migraine can produce transient visual symptoms that classically ‘spread’over minutes. The patient here has sudden visual loss (unusual in migraine) and the constitutional symptoms suggest another cause.

Retinal detachment
Retinal detachment is incorrect. Retinal detachment may cause visual loss, but the overall history is far more in keeping with giant-cell arteritis.

Scleritis
Scleritis is incorrect. Scleritis would have accompanying signs such as redness of the affected eye and it is unlikely to result in acute visual loss.

stem: A 45-year-old woman is found by her Optometrist to have band keratopathy and is referred to the Eye Clinic. Which of the following investigations is likely to be helpful in determining a cause?
explanation:
Serum calcium
Band keratopathy is caused by calcium deposition in Bowman’s layer of the cornea. It can result from the degenerative phase of chronic eye diseases or from hypercalcaemia. Patients who present with band keratopathy should have a serum calcium and phosphate level drawn unless the deposition has been documented previously and a known underlying cause exists. Parathyroid hormone levels should be checked in otherwise idiopathic cases.

Cholesterol
Cholesterol is incorrect. The presence of corneal arcus can be related to hypercholesterolaemia, and is a white encircling band around the cornea.

Ferritin
Ferritin is incorrect. No specific corneal signs are directly related to low ferritin levels, although anecdotally it can cause ocular irritation. Iron levels found on corneas are also called Hudson and Stahli lines, and are not related to plasma serum levels of ferritin.

U&E
U&E is incorrect. Patients with chronic kidney insufficiency who have a corneal finding are usually fortuitous.

Gamma GT
Gamma GT is incorrect. Liver dysfunction can cause problems such as dry eyes, from dysfunctional tear production. 826 Calcium Homeostasis,.

stem: A 49-year-old woman with a history of systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) presents with painless loss of vision in her left eye. On examination her blood pressure is 155/85 mmHg. Ophthalmological examination reveals flame-shaped haemorrhages in all four quadrants of the retina, dilated tortuous retinal veins, cottonwool spots, macular oedema and optic disc swelling. Which one of the following is the most likely cause of her symptoms?
explanation:
Central retinal vein occlusion
Central retinal vein occlusion (CRVO) encompasses retinal changes in all four quadrants, with sudden loss of vision in the affected eye. SLE and hypertension are risk factors for CRVO. This patient requires a cardiovascular screen with appropriate management, with regular follow-up to monitor for neovascularisation of the retina, optic disc, angle and iris.

Branch retinal artery occlusion
Branch retinal artery occlusion is incorrect. This manifests as painless visual field loss. The affected area of the retina would appear pale within a branch distribution, without the other signs seen in this patient.

Branch retinal vein occlusion
Branch retinal vein occlusion is incorrect. This would encompass the same signs as seen in this patient, but would be seen in a branch distribution and not in all four quadrants of the retina.

Central retinal artery occlusion
Central retinal artery occlusion is incorrect. Central retinal artery occlusion would also manifest as sudden, painless loss of vision, however signs include a pale retina, retinal oedema and a “cherry-red spot” at the macula. Retinal Venous Occlusion

Vitreous haemorrhage
Vitreous haemorrhage is incorrect. SLE may cause vitreous haemorrhage in severe cases, causing loss of vision. However, there would be a hazy or limited fundal view which is not mentioned in this scenario. An ultrasound scan would be required in cases of vitreous haemorrhage to ensure there is no retinal detachment.

stem: A 24-year-old woman presents with a history of 10 kg weight loss and is found to be hyperthyroid on biochemical investigation. On examination she has clear proptosis. She is started on carbimazole by the endocrine team. She comes in a week later complaining of gradually reduced visual function. You find her best corrected visual acuities are 6/12 in both eyes and her colour vision is reduced bilaterally; visual fields are normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Dysthyroid optic neuropathy
The typical presentation of thyroid eye disease, which is specific to Graves’ disease, is proptosis, sometimes requiring a corrective lens to allow for the increased refractive error in extremis. While biochemical hyperthyroidism is amenable to treatment, thyroid eye disease rarely recovers and is particularly exacerbated by smoking. In 4-8% of cases, thyroid eye disease can be complicated by optic neuropathy – this is rare, but a very serious complication requiring immediate recognition and prompt treatment with high-dose intravenous steroids. The features, in this case, are clear – optic neuropathy typically presents with loss of colour vision and reduced acuity.

Adverse drug reaction
Adverse drug reaction is incorrect. Carbimazole is not recognised as causing optic neuritis as a side effect. This is sometimes seen in radioiodine treatment, which is still used for the treatment of some thyroid malignancies.

Embolic phenomena
Embolic phenomena is incorrect. These present as sudden, painless visual loss, which can effect either the upper or lower hemisphere of vision in a single visual field, the entire visual field unilaterally or a homonymous hemianopia depending on the level of the visual pathway affected. Colour vision is not reduced and visual acuity loss is total, not reduced.

Multiple sclerosis
Multiple sclerosis is incorrect. This does present with an optic neuritis, but is typically unilateral on presentation and associated with pain on eye movement. The same features of reduced visual acuity and colour vision loss occur, but this is not associated with thyroid disease.

Optic atrophy
Optic atrophy is incorrect. This is a clinical finding, and typically presents after a severe episode of inflammation in the optic nerve. It presents as a pale disc on ophthalmoscopy and is associated with a raft of conditions, including MS, hypertension, glaucoma and central retinal artery occlusion among many others. Useful external weblinks www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC1994768/.

stem: A 64-year-old man with a history of Type 2 diabetes and hypertension comes to the clinic. He awoke from sleep unable to see the top half of the visual field in his right eye. His diabetes is poorly controlled, a recent HbA1c was 76 mmol/mol (9.1%), and his BP on admission to the Emergency Department is 165/105 mmHg. Pulse is 80/min and regular. There is no other focal neurological deficit. What is the most likely cause of this visual field defect?
explanation:
Retinal vascular disease
Hemi-branch retinal vein or artery occlusion can lead to altitudinal defects. It may also be caused by advanced glaucoma. Bilateral cases should raise suspicion of a stroke with bilateral occipital lobe infarcts.

Age-related macular degeneration
Age-related macular degeneration is incorrect. Age-related macular degeneration typically causes loss of central vision, manifesting as a central scotoma. This is usually a gradual process although wet ARMD may cause sudden loss of vision. It would not cause an altitudinal defect.

Parietal lobe infarction
Parietal lobe infarction is incorrect. Parietal lobe lesions cause an inferior homonymous quadrantanopia, although this may progress to a homonymous hemianopia.

Optic chiasm compression
Optic chiasm compression is incorrect. Lesions or compression of the optic chiasm would cause a bitemporal hemianopia.

Temporal lobe infarction
Temporal lobe infarction is incorrect. Temporal lobe lesions would cause a superior homonymous quadrantanopia.

stem: A patient presents with a first episode of a painful reduction in visual acuity in one eye. The acuity is 6/60, ocular movements produce pain and the optic disc is normal. Which one of the following investigations supports the diagnosis of optic neuritis?
explanation:
Abnormal visual evoked potentials (VEP)
In optic neuritis, demyelination causes a reduction in the velocity of the propagation of action potentials and so the VEP response is delayed. The ERG is normal as the retina is unaffected.

Abnormal electroretinogram (ERG)
Abnormal electroretinogram is incorrect. The ERG measures retinal electrical activity and is often used to validate the significance of an abnormal VEP response (ie if the VEP is abnormal but so is the ERG, then the VEP abnormality might be secondary to an eye condition and be a false-positive for optic nerve disease).

Abnormal electro-oculogram (EOG)
Abnormal electro-oculogram is incorrect. The EOG measures the overall electrical activity of the eye and is reduced in degenerative eye conditions affecting the pigment epithelial layer, such as Best’s disease.

Abnormal electroencephalogram (EEG)
Abnormal electroencephalogram is incorrect. An EEG is not an optimal investigation for assessing vision impairment. Optic Neuritis

Abnormal electronystagmogram (ENG)
Abnormal electronystagmogram is incorrect. The ENG is simply a method of documenting nystagmus using the electrical charge of the eye.

stem: A 70-year-old man became wheezy while walking uphill and tripped, hitting his left eye. He now complains of pain in this eye; the cornea is hazy, the globe feels very firm to palpation and there is a hyphaema obscuring most of the iris. Which one of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
explanation:
IV carbonic anhydrase inhibitor
Intravenous carbonic anhydrase inhibitors (such as acetazolamide) can cause adverse reactions (tingling of the fingers is a common side-effect) but will quickly lower the intraocular pressure, before optic nerve damage or even retinal artery compression and occlusion occur. Blunt ocular trauma can have various effects on the eye, including: Subconjunctival haemorrhage Corneal abrasion Traumatic pupillary mydriasis Hyphaema Vitreous haemorrhage Commotio retinae Choroidal rupture Retinal detachment Hyphaema occurs when bleeding from iris vessels fills the anterior chamber with blood and if there is enough blood to settle and form a level of blood. Usually the hyphaema does not fill the entire anterior chamber, but can be described in terms of how far up the posterior corneal surface the level of blood seems to be: 10% or 50%, for example. If the entire anterior chamber is full of blood and no iris can be seen (a 100% hyphaema), the term ‘eight-ball hyphaema’ has been used. Management of hyphaema: Strict rest is vital if a hyphaema is present, as there is an increased risk of a second bleed in the initial period. This is why many do not dilate the pupil in the initial stage, even to get a view of the retina. Hyphaema, if it is large and does not disperse quickly spontaneously (which most do), can cause corneal staining, but the main risk in the acute stage is of raised intraocular pressure (IOP). This occurs as red blood cells clog up the trabecular meshwork, impairing drainage of aqueous humour. One sign of significantly raised IOP is corneal oedema. Endothelial cells on the posterior corneal surface normally maintain corneal transparency. These cells can decompensate in the face of raised IOP and corneal haziness occurs. Although specialist equipment is needed to accurately assess the IOP, palpation can at least give some idea of whether the eye feels very soft, fairly normal or very firm. Digital palpation should not be used if a penetrating injury is suspected.

Examination under anaesthesia
Examination under anaesthesia is incorrect. Examination under anaesthesia might be appropriate if a penetrating injury is seen or suspected, for example if the patient described falling onto a sharp object.

Topical ß-blockers
Topical beta-blockers is incorrect. Topical ß-blockers would lower the IOP, but significant systemic absorption occurs even after the administration of eye drops. A history of dyspnoea on exertion is therefore a contraindication even to topical ß-blockers.

Topical anticholinergics
Topical anticholinergics is incorrect. By avoiding drops that dilate the pupil (such as anticholinergics) the iris remains stable and a second bleed is therefore less likely.

Anterior chamber paracentesis.

stem: A patient is examined in the Diabetic Clinic and is found to have a vitreous haemorrhage, which is precluding a view of his fundus. He is admitted for bed rest. After 3 days the fundus can be visualised. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Proliferative diabetic retinopathy
Vitreous haemorrhage in diabetic patients is commonly caused by bleeding of fragile new vessels of the retina, consistent with neovascularisation in proliferative diabetic retinopathy.

Normal fundi
Normal fundi is incorrect. A diabetic patient with vitreous haemorrhage is extremely unlikely to have a normal fundus.

Background retinopathy
Background retinopathy is incorrect. Micro-aneurysms consistent with background or mild non-proliferative diabetic retinopathy would not cause a vitreous haemorrhage.

Maculopathy
Maculopathy is incorrect. Maculopathy, consisting of macular exudates and haemorrhages, should be considered as a differential as a cause of vitreous haemorrhage, but it is not the most common cause among the listed options.

Pre-proliferative retinopathy.

stem: A 39-year-old man with a history of ulcerative colitis (UC) presents with an acutely painful, red left eye. He is currently managed with mesalazine for his UC and has not suffered an acute attack for some months. On examination his BP is 150/92 mmHg and his pulse is 90 beats per minute and regular. Visual acuity is reduced to 6/9 in the left eye, and is 6/6 in the right eye. There is conjunctival injection, mostly peri-limbal, with cells 2+ and flare in the anterior chamber. The vitreous is clear with no fundal involvement. Which one of the following is the most appropriate initial treatment?
explanation:
Prednisolone eye drops
The history of a red, painful eye in the presence of anterior chamber cells and flare suggests a diagnosis of acute anterior uveitis, which is associated with inflammatory bowel disease. The mainstay of treatment is intensive prednisolone eye drop therapy for a number of weeks. Cyclopentolate eye drops are usually prescribed in addition for a few days to help with pain and to prevent posterior synechiae (adhesions of the iris to the lens capsule) from forming.

Acetazolamide
Acetazolomide is incorrect. Acetazolomide is a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor used to reduce intra-ocular pressure in open-angle glaucoma, secondary glaucoma, and peri-operatively in angle-closure glaucoma. It is taken by mouth or by intravenous injection. This patient’s symptoms are not suggestive of glaucoma.

Chloramphenicol eye drops
Chloramphenicol eye drops is incorrect. Chloramphenicol is used to treat superficial eye infections. Most cases of acute bacterial conjunctivitis are self-limiting; where treatment is appropriate, antibacterial eye drops or an eye ointment is used. A poor response might indicate viral or allergic conjunctivitis. However, this patient has a history suggestive of uveitis.

Timolol eye drops
Timolol eye drops is incorrect. Timolol eye drops are beta blocker drops used to treat ocular hypertension and open-angle glaucoma. It works to decrease aqueous humour production and therefore pressure inside the eye. This patient’s history is not suggestive of glaucoma.

Viscotears eye drops
Viscotears eye drops is incorrect. Viscotears drops are artificial tear drops used in the management of dry eye conditions. stem: A 30-year-old woman presents to clinic with painful loss of vision affecting her right eye. She says that the vision has become progressively more blurred over the past five days with an associated headache. There is a past medical history of hypertension and Type 2 diabetes diagnosed 2 years earlier. She is a current smoker. On examination, visual acuity is decreased in the right eye with reduced colour vision as demonstrated with the Ishihara test. Pain is elicited on testing ocular movements. Visual field testing reveals a central scotoma in the right eye. Fundal examination shows swelling of the right eye optic disc with an otherwise normal retina and macula. Blood pressure is 160/90. Which one of the following is the most likely cause of her right eye symptoms?
explanation:
Optic neuritis
Reduced visual acuity, loss of colour vision, a central scotoma and optic disc swelling are all markers of optic nerve dysfunction. The lack of other fundal abnormalities in addition to painful eye movements is typical of optic neuritis. This patient requires a full neurological work-up to look for potential causes such as multiple sclerosis. High dose corticosteroids may be an option to reduce the time it takes for her vision to recover in the short-term, however they have no long-term benefit to vision.

Central retinal artery occlusion
Central retinal artery occlusion is incorrect. This typically presents as sudden, painless loss of vision, unlike the history given above. Additionally, the retina would appear pale with a “cherry red spot” in the macula.

Central retinal vein occlusion
Central retinal vein occlusion is incorrect. This patient has risk factors for a central retinal vein occlusion (CRVO) including diabetes, hypertension and a history of smoking. However, similar to central retinal artery occlusion, CRVO presents as sudden, painless loss of vision. Whilst the optic disc may be swollen, fundal examination would also reveal flame-shaped haemorrhages, dilated veins with tortuosity and cotton-wool spots.

Diabetic retinopathy
Diabetic retinopathy is incorrect. Whilst the patient is a known type 2 diabetic, diabetic retinopathy does not usually cause loss of vision unless there is neovascularisation and/or vitreous haemorrhage, a retinal detachment or macula oedema. This patient has a normal macula and retina which excludes the possibility of diabetic retinopathy and associated complications.

Hypertensive retinopathy
Hypertensive retinopathy is incorrect. Hypertensive retinopathy may lead to vision loss if there is macula oedema or optic disc swelling. Optic disc swelling represents Grade 4 hypertensive retinopathy. Again, the lack of other fundal features makes this option less likely. This includes arteriolar narrowing, arterio-venous crossing or “nipping”, retinal flame haemorrhages and exudates. Loss of vision from hypertension would typically be painless.

stem: A 42-year-old man with a history of Type 2 diabetes and hypertension comes to the Emergency department for review. He is a contact lens wearer and he has pain, photophobia and decreased vision in his left eye after accidentally leaving his contact lens in situ overnight. He wears monthly soft lenses and admits he does not clean them each time before and after use. On examination he has reduced visual acuity in the left eye to 6/24, with diffuse conjunctival injection and corneal haze. There is a 2x2mm circular opacity near the central cornea which stains with fluorescein dye, surrounded by an infiltrate. The anterior chamber has cells 2+. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Infective keratitis
The symptoms and signs in this contact-lens wearer are highly typical of infective or microbial keratitis. The risk increases with poor contact lens hygiene and use, including swimming or showering in contact lenses and sleeping in them. This is exacerbated with his history of diabetes which would predispose him to infection. A 2x2mm ulcer would need to be scraped for histopathology analysis prior to commencing antimicrobial therapy, including acanthomoeba which is more prevalent in contact lens wearers. He should then be commenced on intensive topical antibiotics plus analgesia, with a view to review with pathology results within 48 hours.

Corneal abrasion
Corneal abrasion is incorrect. A corneal abrasion would also cause pain and photophobia, however would not cause an infiltrate. A corneal abrasion is a superficial epithelial defect. This does not require a corneal scrape and may be treated with less intensive antibiotic treatment and lubricants.

Glaucoma
Glaucoma is incorrect. Acute angle closure glaucoma may cause an acutely painful, red eye with corneal haze and reduced visual acuity. However, this is not consistent with the 2x2mm opacity described in this scenario which is typical of infective keratitis. Patients with acute angle closure glaucoma are usually nauseous and/or vomiting, with a mid-dilated pupil.

Hypopyon
Hypopyon is incorrect. A hypopyon is a clinical sign, not a diagnosis. It refers to accumulation of white blood cells in the anterior chamber, and is most commonly caused by severe infective keratitis and uveitis. It is not mentioned in the above scenario and thus presumed to be absent.

Sjogren’s syndrome
Sjogren’s syndrome is incorrect. Sjogren’s syndrome causes dry eye (keratoconjunctivitis sicca) which may cause an irritated, red eye. This is typically bilateral. Whilst dry eye may lead to corneal complications if chronic and severe, there is nothing in the history to suggest this as the underlying cause. Corneal ulcers and keratitis.

stem: A 21-year-old man presents to the Emergency department. He has double vision on looking to the left. There is no past medical history of note. On examination his BP is 110/70 mmHg, pulse is 70/min and regular. Upon examination of ocular movements, the patient is unable to abduct his left eye. Diplopia with horizontal separation of images is evoked when attempting to look left, and is worse when looking into the distance. Upon covering the left eye, the outer image disappears. Weakness of which of the following muscles is most likely responsible for his symptoms?
explanation:
Left lateral rectus
Loss of unilateral abduction is consistent with a sixth nerve palsy, which innervates the lateral rectus muscle. Additionally, it is important to remember 3 rules: double vision is maximal in the direction of gaze of the affected eye, the false image is the outer image, and the false image arises in the affected eye. Therefore, an isolated sixth nerve palsy leading to paralysis of the left lateral rectus is by far the most likely diagnosis. The most common cause in an adult is microvascular, however with this patients’ young age and absence of medical history other causes such as a neoplasm, raised intracranial pressure and infection become more likely, although it may simply be idiopathic.

Left medial rectus
Left medial rectus is incorrect. The medial rectus is innervated by the third nerve and a palsy would cause weakness of adduction, not abduction as in this case. Additionally, the third nerve also innervates the superior and inferior rectus, the inferior oblique, the ciliary ganglion and the levator palpebrae superioris. A third nerve palsy would thus typically cause ptosis and a dilated pupil, which are not present in this scenario.

Left superior oblique
Left superior oblique is incorrect. The superior oblique muscle is innervated by the fourth nerve. A fourth nerve palsy, which is rare in itself, would cause vertical diplopia which is worse on looking down. They may have a head tilt to the opposite side of gaze with chin depression to compensate.

Right lateral rectus
Right lateral rectus is incorrect. The left eye in this scenario is unable to abduct, not the right eye. A 40-old woman with AIDS presents to the genitourinary clinic with a shadow in her vision in one eye. Which one of the following supports a diagnosis of cytomegalovirus (CMV) retinitis?

Right medial rectus
Right medial rectus is incorrect. The left eye is clearly the abnormal eye with weakness of abduction and worsening of diplopia when looking to the left. The medial rectus is not affected here as explained in Option B.
